entries.title: Turning effect of force and principle of moments

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students use the actual distance from the pivot to the point of application of the force, instead of the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force. The moment formula uses the perpendicular distance -- the shortest distance from the pivot to the line along which the force acts. If the force is applied at an angle to the lever arm, the perpendicular distance is less than the actual distance.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: When a force is applied at an angle to the lever arm, students are unsure whether to use sin or cos. The perpendicular distance = actual distance x sin(theta) where theta is the angle between the lever arm and the force direction. So moment = F x d x sin(theta) = F x (perpendicular distance). Students often incorrectly use cos instead of sin.

student_says: sum of forces = 0 for balance
total force on both sides equal
balanced means forces are equal
see-saw mein dono side ka force same
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: For rotational equilibrium, it is the sum of moments (not forces) that must balance. The principle of moments states: sum of clockwise moments = sum of anticlockwise moments. Equal forces on both sides do NOT guarantee balance if they are at different distances from the pivot. A light child far from the centre can balance a heavier child closer to the centre.

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Centre of gravity

classification_patterns.pattern: where is CG of a ring

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students assume the centre of gravity must always lie within the material of the body. The CG is a point determined by mass distribution, not by where the material is. For a uniform ring, the CG is at the centre -- which is empty space. For an L-shaped or boomerang-shaped object, the CG can lie outside the body entirely. The CG is simply the point where the entire weight appears to act, regardless of whether that point is occupied by material.

student_says: CG and CM are the same
centre of gravity = centre of mass
no difference between CG and CM

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Centre of gravity and centre of mass are the same only for uniform gravitational fields (near Earth's surface). The CM depends on mass distribution; the CG depends on mass distribution AND gravitational field. They coincide in most everyday situations, but technically they are different concepts. In the context of Class 10 ICSE, they are treated as equivalent for practical purposes.

student_says: CG lies on axis of symmetry

CG must be on the axis
CG axis of symmetry par hoga
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: While CG does lie on any axis of symmetry, students incorrectly assume that having an axis of symmetry uniquely determines the CG position. For example, in a uniform triangular lamina, the CG is at the centroid (intersection of medians), not simply 'on the axis.' The CG lies at the geometric centroid for uniform bodies, which requires knowledge of the specific shape.

entries.title: Types of equilibrium (stable, unstable, neutral)

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students often confuse 'stable equilibrium' with 'a body that is simply not moving.' A body at rest could be in stable, unstable, or neutral equilibrium -- what matters is what happens after a slight displacement, not whether it is currently moving. A cone balanced perfectly on its apex is momentarily at rest, but it is in unstable equilibrium, not stable. The test is always: displace slightly and observe.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students often mix up the CG test: in stable equilibrium, the CG RISES on slight displacement (and falls back); in unstable, the CG FALLS further away (and keeps falling); in neutral, the CG stays at the same height. Students commonly reverse stable and unstable, thinking stable = CG falls (confusing it with a ball rolling downhill being 'stable').

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students confuse neutral equilibrium with unstable equilibrium or think it means 'perfectly balanced at one point.' Neutral equilibrium means: on slight displacement, the body stays in the new position without returning (like a ball on a flat surface). It does NOT roll back (not stable) and it does NOT fall further (not unstable). A cylinder on its curved side is neutral -- push it and it stays put at the new spot.

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Lenses (convex and concave, ray diagrams, lens formula)

classification_patterns.pattern: how to draw ray diagram for concave lens

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students incorrectly use 1/f = 1/u + 1/v for lenses. With the Cartesian sign convention the correct form is 1/f = 1/v - 1/u. Because a real object has u negative, substituting the signed value turns the minus into a plus, which numerically looks like 1/f = 1/v + 1/u but the sign convention must be applied consistently. Using 1/f = 1/v + 1/u without signs gives wrong results for virtual images and concave lenses. This was explicitly flagged by CISCE examiners in 2019.

student_says: concave lens converges light
convex lens diverges light
concave is converging lens
convex concave yaad nahi rehta
which lens converges and which diverges
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students frequently confuse which lens converges and which diverges light. Convex (thick in middle) converges parallel rays to a real focus; concave (thin in middle) diverges parallel rays as if from a virtual focus. The mnemonic 'convex converges, concave diverges' helps. Students also mix up the shape: 'fat in middle = converge, thin in middle = diverge.'

student_says: convex lens has negative focal length
concave lens has positive focal length
focal length of concave lens is positive
concave lens ka f positive hai
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Under the Cartesian sign convention, the focal length of a convex lens is positive (+) because the focus is on the opposite side of the incident light. The focal length of a concave lens is negative (-) because the virtual focus is on the same side as the incident light. Students consistently reverse these signs, leading to wrong numerical answers.

entries.title: Power of a lens and magnifying glass

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students believe power is always a positive number. Correction: Power carries the sign of the focal length. A convex lens has positive power (e.g., +2 D); a concave lens has negative power (e.g., -4 D). CISCE examiners (2025, Question 5) repeatedly observed candidates 'applying the wrong sign convention/substitution' in lens numericals -- forgetting the negative sign for a concave lens loses the marks.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students confuse the relationship between power and focal length. Power is the reciprocal of focal length: P = 1/f. A short focal length means high power (strong bending); a long focal length means low power (weak bending). A thick, fat lens has a short focal length and therefore HIGH power, not low power.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students may not understand the definition properly. 1 dioptre (1 D) is the power of a lens whose focal length is 1 metre. Power in dioptres = 1 / focal length in metres. If f = 0.5 m, P = 2 D. If f = -0.25 m, P = -4 D. The sign follows the focal length sign.

entries.title: Dispersion and the visible spectrum

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: The order of colours is a result, not a cause. Red is deviated least because it has the longest wavelength (about 7000 angstrom) and therefore the smallest refractive index in glass; since deviation depends on refractive index, red bends least. The 2024 CISCE PPA specifically noted students giving 'because it is the first colour' or 'because it is the strongest' as reasons -- both are incorrect causal explanations. The wavelength-refractive index link is the correct chain of reasoning.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Dispersion is the splitting of white light into its constituent colours by a prism (or raindrop), caused by different refractive indices for different wavelengths. Scattering is the random redirection of light by particles in the medium. The 2020 and 2023 CISCE examiners explicitly flagged candidates who used 'dispersion' or 'reflection' instead of 'scattering' to explain the blue sky. These are distinct phenomena with different mechanisms.

entries.title: Work done (W = FS cos theta)

classification_patterns.pattern: what is work done in physics

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students think that carrying a heavy bag horizontally involves doing work on the bag, because it feels tiring. Mechanical work done on the bag is zero because the upward force (equal to the weight) is perpendicular to the horizontal displacement (theta = 90 deg, cos 90 deg = 0). The tiredness is a biological/physiological effect in the muscles, not mechanical work on the object. Work = 0 because force and displacement are perpendicular.

student_says: pushing a wall is work done

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students think exerting a force means work is done. Work requires BOTH force AND displacement in the direction of the force. If you push a wall and it doesn't move, displacement = 0, so work done = 0 regardless of how much force you apply. Similarly, holding a heavy object stationary involves zero mechanical work even though you get tired.

how to use cos theta in work formula

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students may know the formula W = F*S*cos(theta) but struggle with correctly identifying the angle theta. Theta is the angle between the direction of the force and the direction of displacement. When theta = 0, cos(0) = 1, maximum work. When theta = 90, cos(90) = 0, zero work. When theta = 180, cos(180) = -1, negative work (force opposes motion).

entries.title: Power and its relation to work

A 100 W bulb and a 60 W bulb running for the same time consume different amounts of energy (100 W uses more), but a 60 W bulb running for twice as long as a 100 W bulb can use the same total energy. Power = work/time; total energy = power x time.

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Conservation of energy (U + K = constant)

classification_patterns.pattern: pendulum stops so energy is not conserved

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students think energy is 'lost' when a pendulum eventually stops swinging, violating conservation of energy. Energy is not lost -- it is converted to heat (due to air resistance and friction at the pivot) and sound. The total energy including these forms is still conserved; only the mechanical energy (U + K) decreases. In our idealised verification (neglecting air resistance), U + K remains constant at every point.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students think a freely falling body gains total energy as it falls. In free fall (neglecting air resistance), potential energy decreases while kinetic energy increases by the same amount. Total energy (U + K) remains constant throughout the fall. At the top: all U, no K. In the middle: some U, some K. At the bottom: all K, no U. But U + K is always the same.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students believe all electromagnetic waves need a medium to travel, like sound waves do. EM waves are transverse oscillations of electric and magnetic fields and do NOT require a medium -- they travel through vacuum at 3 x 10^8 m/s, which is why sunlight reaches Earth across empty space. Sound waves are mechanical waves and need a medium; EM waves do not. This is one of the most fundamental distinctions in wave physics.

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Scattering of light

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students believe the sky is blue because of dispersion of light. This was explicitly flagged by CISCE examiners in 2020 and again in 2023. Correction: Dispersion is the splitting of white light into its colours by a prism (or raindrop), caused by different refractive indices for different wavelengths. Scattering is the independent redirection of light by particles in the medium. The blue sky is caused by Rayleigh scattering -- shorter wavelengths (blue/violet) are scattered more by air molecules than longer wavelengths. Violet is scattered most but our eyes are less sensitive to it.

student_says: shorter wavelength means less scattering

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students reverse or misunderstand the wavelength-scattering relationship. Scattering is inversely proportional to the fourth power of wavelength: shorter wavelengths are scattered much more. Blue light (~450 nm) is scattered about 10 times more than red light (~700 nm). This is why the sky is blue -- blue light is scattered in all directions by air molecules. At sunset, light passes through more atmosphere, so blue is scattered away and only red/orange reaches our eyes.

entries.title: Reflection of sound waves and echoes

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students use distance = speed x time directly without dividing by 2. Correction: The time measured in an echo problem is the time for the sound to go to the obstacle AND come back, so the round-trip distance is v x t and the one-way distance is (v x t)/2. CISCE examiners have repeatedly observed that candidates substitute into formulas without understanding which quantity is the round trip; the same careless mistake occurs in radar problems. Always remember: measured time = to + fro, so actual distance = (v x t)/2.

If time is given in seconds and distance is needed in meters, use v = 340 m/s. If the problem requires km/hr, convert: 340 m/s = 340 x 18/5 = 1224 km/hr. Using mixed units (km/hr with seconds) is a common source of wrong answers in CISCE numericals.

Correction: Loudness is the subjective sensation in the listener's ear; intensity is the objective, instrument-measurable quantity (energy per unit area per unit time, W/m^2). Loudness depends on the sensitivity of the ear and varies from person to person; intensity is the same for everyone measuring it. entries.title: Mechanical advantage (MA = L/E)

By the law of conservation of energy, if the machine multiplies force, it must divide distance by the same factor. You apply a small effort over a larger distance; the load moves a smaller distance. A steady DC current produces a constant magnetic flux in the core; since there is no change in flux, no emf is induced in the secondary (Faraday's law requires changing flux). misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Step-up transformer: more turns in secondary (Ns > Np), so secondary voltage > primary voltage. Step-down transformer: fewer turns in secondary (Ns < Np), so secondary voltage < primary voltage. Ns/Np = Vs/Vp.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: A transformer has NO moving parts. It works purely on electromagnetic induction through stationary coils wound on a stationary core. It is completely different from a generator or motor which have moving parts.

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Latent heat and change of state

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: During melting (at 0 deg C) and boiling (at 100 deg C at 1 atm), temperature stays CONSTANT. The heat energy is used to break inter-particle bonds (potential energy increases), NOT to increase kinetic energy (temperature). Only after the phase change is complete does temperature rise again.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: A large amount of heat (latent heat) is required at the melting point to break the bonds. The temperature does not rise, but heat IS being absorbed continuously. This hidden heat is the 'latent' heat. Without supplying this heat, melting cannot proceed.

student_says: latent heat of fusion and vaporization same

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Latent heat of vaporization is MUCH larger than latent heat of fusion. For water, Lf = 336 kJ/kg and Lv = 2260 kJ/kg. Vaporization requires breaking ALL intermolecular bonds, while fusion only loosens them. Boiling needs about 6.7 times more heat per kg than melting.

latent heat does not exist

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Latent means 'hidden' because the heat does not cause a temperature change — it is hidden in the sense that a thermometer does not detect it. But the heat is very real and measurable. It goes into increasing the potential energy of particles by breaking bonds, not increasing kinetic energy (temperature).

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Efficiency = (MA / VR) × 100. Since MA < VR for any real machine (due to friction), MA must be in the numerator to get a result less than 100%. misconception_signatures.why_wrong: No real machine can ever achieve 100% efficiency. Even with the best design, there is always some friction between moving parts, some air resistance, some heat loss. The theoretical limit approaches 100% but never reaches it. Only an ideal (imaginary) frictionless machine would have 100% efficiency, and that does not exist in reality.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: MA and efficiency are different concepts. MA is a force ratio (L/E), while efficiency is a ratio of output work to input work (MA/VR). A machine can have high MA but low efficiency if VR is very large. Efficiency depends on both MA and VR.

entries.title: Levers (classes I, II, III with MA and VR)

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: The classification rule is simple: identify which of the three components (Fulcrum, Load, Effort) is BETWEEN the other two. Fulcrum in the middle = Class I (seesaw). Load in the middle = Class II (bottle opener, wheelbarrow). Effort in the middle = Class III (tweezers, human arm). misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Only Class I and Class II levers are force multipliers (MA > 1). Class III levers are speed/distance multipliers where MA < 1 because the effort arm is shorter than the load arm. In Class III, you apply a larger force but get a greater speed/distance of movement (e.g., human arm, fishing rod, tweezers).

Examples: human forearm (fulcrum = elbow, effort from biceps between fulcrum and load in hand), tweezers, fishing rod, broom.

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Nuclear fission

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Fission and fusion are opposite processes. Fission splits a heavy nucleus (like U-235) into two lighter nuclei. Fusion combines two light nuclei (like hydrogen isotopes) into a heavier nucleus (helium). Both release energy via mass defect but through opposite mechanisms. This confusion was explicitly noted in CISCE examiner reports.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Mass is NOT conserved in nuclear reactions. A small amount of mass (mass defect) is converted to energy according to E = mc^2. The total mass of fission products + emitted neutrons is less than the original mass of U-235 + neutron. This 'missing mass' is released as enormous energy.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: U-235 undergoes fission most readily with slow (thermal) neutrons, not fast neutrons. Fast neutrons may pass through without causing fission. This is why moderators (graphite, heavy water) are used in reactors to slow down neutrons, increasing the probability of fission.

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Total internal reflection and critical angle

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: TIR ONLY occurs when light travels from a DENSER to a RARER medium. When light goes from rarer to dense, it bends TOWARDS the normal, so the angle of refraction is always less than the angle of incidence — it can never reach 90 degrees, so TIR cannot happen. TIR requires the refracted angle to reach 90 degrees, which only happens when going from dense to rare.

at critical angle refracted ray bends 45 degrees
critical angle means light stops
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: At the critical angle, the angle of refraction is exactly 90 degrees (the refracted ray travels along the boundary). The angle of incidence is the critical angle. For angles of incidence greater than the critical angle, total internal reflection occurs and there is NO refracted ray at all.

student_says: higher critical angle means higher refractive index
critical angle and refractive index are directly proportional
if critical angle increases refractive index also increases
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: sin(c) = 1/μ, so c = arcsin(1/μ). A higher refractive index (denser medium) means a SMALLER critical angle. Diamond has μ ≈ 2.42, so its critical angle is only about 24 degrees — very small. Air to water has μ ≈ 1.33, critical angle ≈ 49 degrees. Higher μ → smaller critical angle. They are inversely related.

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Refraction of light through glass block

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: The emergent ray is PARALLEL to the incident ray but displaced sideways (lateral displacement). It is NOT in the same straight line. The ray bends towards the normal when entering glass (air → glass, slower medium), then bends away from the normal when leaving glass (glass → air, faster medium). Since the two faces of a rectangular glass block are parallel, the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray but shifted sideways.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Apparent depth is always LESS than real depth. When light travels from water (dense) to air (rare), it bends AWAY from the normal, making the bottom appear shallower. Apparent depth = Real depth / μ (refractive index). Since μ > 1, apparent depth < real depth. This is why a swimming pool looks shallower than it is.

Snell's law has refraction angle on left for first medium
sin i / sin r = n2/n1
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Snell's law: n1 sin(i) = n2 sin(r), where i is the angle in the FIRST medium and r is the angle in the SECOND medium. Alternatively, n2/n1 = sin(i)/sin(r). The ratio of sines equals the ratio of refractive indices. Swapping i and r reverses the relationship.

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Refractive index and its relationship to speed, wavelength, frequency

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: The frequency of light remains CONSTANT during refraction. Frequency is determined by the source and does not change when light crosses a boundary. Only speed and wavelength change. If frequency changed, the colour of light would appear different in different media, which does not happen. The relationship is: v = f × λ, and since v changes but f is constant, λ must change.

student_says: refractive index can be less than 1
refractive index of vacuum is 0
n can be negative
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: The absolute refractive index of any medium is always ≥ 1. Vacuum has n = 1 (minimum possible value). Air has n ≈ 1.0003. All other materials have n > 1 because light always travels slowest in vacuum. Relative refractive index (n21 = n2/n1) can be less than 1 when going from a denser to a rarer medium, but the absolute refractive index of any material is always greater than 1.

student_says: wavelength stays same speed changes

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: When light enters a new medium: speed (v) changes, wavelength (λ) changes, but frequency (f) stays constant. The new wavelength λ' = λ/n, where n is the refractive index. The new speed v' = c/n. Frequency is the bridge between them: v = f × λ always holds, and since f is fixed, v and λ must change together proportionally.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: The correct symbol is 'kg' — lowercase 'k' for prefix kilo, lowercase 'g' for gram. ONLY symbols derived from scientists' names are capitalised: Ampere (A), Kelvin (K), Newton (N), Tesla (T). For all other units, use lowercase: metre (m), second (s), kilogram (kg), mole (mol), candela (cd). This was repeatedly flagged in CISCE examiner reports for careless case conventions.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: CGS: centimetre-gram-second (length in cm, mass in g, time in s). FPS: foot-pound-second (length in ft, mass in lb, time in s). MKS: metre-kilogram-second. SI (MKSA): metre-kilogram-second-ampere, plus kelvin, mole, candela. Students often mix up which unit belongs to which system.

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Vector addition (triangle law, parallelogram law)

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: P + Q is only the magnitude of the resultant when vectors are parallel (θ = 0°). In general, R = √(P² + Q² + 2PQ cos θ). The resultant depends on the angle between vectors. For perpendicular vectors (θ = 90°), R = √(P² + Q²). For opposite vectors (θ = 180°), R = |P - Q|. This was flagged in the 2025 CISCE PPA report.

resultant is always the biggest

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: The resultant magnitude depends on the angle. R can be greater than, equal to, or less than either P or Q. When vectors are opposite (θ = 180°), R = |P - Q| which can be less than both. When θ > 90°, R can be less than the larger vector. Maximum R = P + Q (parallel), minimum R = |P - Q| (anti-parallel).

student_says: direction doesn't matter in vector addition
we only need magnitudes
vector sum is just adding magnitudes
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Direction is the defining property of vectors. Two vectors of equal magnitude but opposite directions cancel to zero. Vector addition must account for both magnitude AND direction. The triangle/parallelogram laws exist precisely because direction matters.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: The resultant vector has the same unit as the original vectors (e.g., if P and Q are in newtons, R is in newtons). The angle θ is dimensionless (measured in degrees or radians, not a physical unit). The direction (angle) of the resultant is also dimensionless.

Efficiency measures how much of the input becomes useful OUTPUT WORK. COP measures how much useful HEAT is moved per unit of input WORK. entries.title: Two-dimensional collisions (oblique impact)

classification_patterns.pattern: e applies to normal component only

why only normal component for restitution

student_says: e = (v2 - v1)/(u1 - u2) using full vectors
e applies to relative velocity vector
coefficient of restitution on whole velocity
e = change in velocity / initial velocity
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: e is defined ONLY along the line of impact (normal direction). Only the normal components of velocity appear: e = -(v2n - v1n)/(u2n - u1n). The tangential components are completely unaffected because the surfaces are smooth (no tangential force). Using full velocity vectors gives wrong equations and wrong answers.

student_says: tangential force acts during smooth collision
friction acts tangentially in collision
tangential component changes in collision
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: By definition, smooth surfaces have NO friction or tangential force. Only the NORMAL force acts during the collision. Therefore, the tangential component of velocity is completely unchanged for each particle: v1t = u1t and v2t = u2t. Only the normal components change.

student_says: line of impact is the line of motion
line of impact is the line joining centers always
any line can be line of impact
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: The line of impact is specifically the common normal line at the point of contact — it is perpendicular to the tangent plane at the contact point. It is NOT necessarily the line joining the centers (that's only true for spheres). The line of impact is the direction along which the impulsive force acts.

student_says: head-on and oblique collision same formula
oblique is just head-on at an angle
same equations apply to both
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: In a head-on (1D) collision, all velocities are along the line of impact so normal = full velocity. In oblique (2D) collision, you must split each velocity into normal and tangential components first. The tangential components never enter the restitution or momentum equations. This splitting is the key step students miss.

student_says: momentum conserved only along line of impact
tangential momentum not conserved
only normal direction conserves momentum
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Momentum is conserved along BOTH the line of impact AND the tangent direction. There is no external force along either direction. Conservation along the tangent gives v1t = u1t and v2t = u2t directly. Conservation along the normal gives the standard 1D momentum equation using normal components.

entries.title: Torricelli's theorem and velocity of efflux

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: In v = sqrt(2gh), density rho cancels out completely during the Bernoulli derivation. Both hydrostatic pressure (rho*g*h) and dynamic pressure (1/2*rho*v^2) contain rho, so it divides out. Mercury and water at the same depth h emerge at the same speed. Density only affects the pressure, not the efflux speed.

area of hole changes efflux speed
larger hole velocity is higher

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: The efflux VELOCITY v = sqrt(2gh) is independent of the hole size. Only the VOLUMETRIC FLOW RATE (Q = A*v) depends on area. A bigger hole lets more water out per second but each drop still exits at the same speed sqrt(2gh). This is a critical distinction between speed and flow rate.

student_says: pressure at hole is atmospheric so zero
pressure at outlet is zero
gauge pressure at hole is zero
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: The gauge pressure at the hole IS atmospheric (zero gauge), but the pressure at the free surface is NOT zero — it is rho*g*h above atmospheric. It is this pressure difference rho*g*h that drives the flow. Both sides of Bernoulli's equation must use the SAME reference (both gauge or both absolute).

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: As the tank empties, h (the depth of the hole below the free surface) decreases, so v = sqrt(2gh) decreases. The efflux speed is only constant if the tank is being refilled to maintain constant h. For a draining tank, v decreases as sqrt(h) decreases.

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Non-inertial frames and pseudo force

classification_patterns.pattern: centripetal and centrifugal are action reaction

student_says: centrifugal and centripetal are action reaction

centripetal and centrifugal are Newton's third law pair
centrifugal balances centripetal
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Newton's third law pairs must act on TWO DIFFERENT BODIES. Centripetal force (e.g., tension) acts on the revolving body. Its reaction (e.g., the body pulling on the string) acts on the string/center. Centrifugal force, if it exists at all, acts on the SAME body as centripetal — in the rotating frame. They are not a pair. They cannot both exist as action-reaction.

student_says: pseudo force acts in all frames
centrifugal force is real
pseudo force can be measured
pseudo force exists in inertial frame
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Pseudo force exists ONLY in non-inertial (accelerating/rotating) frames. In an inertial frame, the same situation is explained by real forces alone. Pseudo force is a mathematical correction to make Newton's laws work in a non-inertial frame — it is not a real physical force and cannot be measured or felt independently.

student_says: pseudo force always opposite to acceleration
pseudo force is -ma always
pseudo force direction is always backward
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Pseudo force = -m*a_frame, where a_frame is the acceleration of the non-inertial frame. It acts in the direction OPPOSITE to the frame's acceleration. If the frame accelerates UP, pseudo force acts DOWN. If the frame accelerates to the RIGHT, pseudo force acts to the LEFT. Students often get the sign wrong in lift problems.

student_says: feeling heavier means more gravity
apparent weight increase is real
normal force equals mg even in accelerating lift
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: When a lift accelerates upward, you feel heavier because the floor pushes you harder (N = m(g+a)), NOT because gravity increased. Gravity is still g. The increased normal force is the floor responding to the acceleration. In free fall (a = g downward), N = 0 and you feel weightless — gravity still acts but nothing pushes back.

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Law of limiting factors (Blackman's law)

classification_patterns.pattern: all factors together limit the rate

student_says: rate is average of all factors

rate = sum of factors / number of factors

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Blackman's law states that the rate equals the MINIMUM of the individual factor ceilings, not an average or sum. Only the factor in shortest supply limits the rate at any instant. Increasing a non-limiting factor does nothing — like pouring more water into a bucket with a small hole; the extra water just overflows.

student_says: more light always increases photosynthesis
more CO2 always helps
increasing temperature always speeds up reaction
all factors are equally important
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: If light is already saturating and CO2 is limiting, increasing light intensity does NOTHING to the rate. Only when you remove the current limiting factor (increase CO2) does the rate increase — until another factor becomes limiting. You must address the bottleneck, not boost everything.

student_says: Blackman and Liebig same law
Liebig's law of minimum is same as Blackman's
both say the minimum factor limits
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: While both laws describe limiting factors, they have different origins and slightly different framing. Liebig's Law of the Minimum (1840) applies specifically to soil nutrients in agriculture — the nutrient in shortest supply limits growth. Blackman's Law (1905) is broader, applying to any multi-factor rate process like photosynthesis with light, CO2, temperature, etc.

student_says: same factor always limits
CO2 is always the limiting factor
light is always limiting in photosynthesis
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: The limiting factor CHANGES as conditions change. At low light, light is limiting. As you increase light, CO2 may become limiting. At very high light and CO2, temperature may become limiting. The limiting factor is the one in shortest supply RELATIVE to its saturation point at any given condition.

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Resolution of vectors and rectangular components

Ay is always A sin theta
x component is always cosine
y component is always sine
cos for x and sin for y always
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: The component along the axis from which the angle is measured takes COSINE, and the perpendicular component takes SINE. If theta is measured from the x-axis: Ax = A cos(theta), Ay = A sin(theta). If theta is measured from the y-axis: Ay = A cos(theta), Ax = A sin(theta). Always check which axis the angle is referenced to.

Ax > A is possible
cosine can be greater than 1 somehow
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Both |cos(theta)| <= 1 and |sin(theta)| <= 1 always, so |Ax| = |A cos(theta)| <= A and |Ay| = |A sin(theta)| <= A. A component can NEVER exceed the original vector magnitude. If a student gets |Ax| > A, they have swapped sin and cos or measured the wrong angle.

student_says: component is always positive
magnitude is always positive so component is positive
Ax and Ay are always positive values
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Components are signed quantities based on the chosen coordinate direction. Ax = A cos(theta) can be negative if theta > 90 degrees or theta < -90 degrees. The sign indicates direction. Always track which quadrant the vector lies in — sin and cos signs change by quadrant.

student_says: resolution is same as projection
component is projection of vector on axis
resolution and projection are identical
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Resolution breaks a vector into two perpendicular components whose vector sum equals the original. Projection is the scalar component (signed length along one axis). Resolution gives BOTH components (vector form), while projection gives only ONE scalar. They are related but not identical concepts.

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Scalar (dot) product

classification_patterns.pattern: what is scalar product of vectors
dot product vs cross product difference

student_says: dot product gives a vector
dot product has direction
a.b is a vector quantity

dot product direction is same as a
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: The dot product a·b = ab cos(theta) involves only magnitudes (scalars) and cosine (scalar). The result is a pure scalar — a number with a unit, no direction. This is exactly why it is CALLED the scalar product. If the result had direction, it would be a vector product.

student_says: dot product and cross product same thing
dot product = cross product
dot and cross product give same result
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Dot product: a·b = ab cos(theta), scalar, commutative (a·b = b·a). Cross product: a×b = ab sin(theta) n, vector, anti-commutative (a×b = -(b×a)). They are completely different operations with different formulas, different results (scalar vs vector), and different properties.

student_says: dot product uses sin theta
a.b = ab sin theta
dot product has sine in formula
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: The dot product uses COSINE: a·b = ab cos(theta). The cross product uses SINE: |a×b| = ab sin(theta). Students frequently mix them up. A mnemonic: 'dot' product measures how much two arrows point in the SAME direction (cosine measures alignment), while 'cross' product measures how much they TILT relative to each other (sine measures tilt).

student_says: dot product zero means vectors perpendicular
zero dot product means 90 degrees only
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: While perpendicular vectors (theta = 90°) DO have zero dot product, the converse is also true: if a·b = 0, then either theta = 90° OR a = 0 OR b = 0. A zero vector dotted with any vector gives zero. Students should check if either vector is zero before concluding perpendicularity.

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Vector (cross) product

classification_patterns.pattern: what is cross product of vectors

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: The cross product is ANTI-commutative: a×b = -(b×a). Swapping the order reverses the direction of the unit vector n (by the right-hand rule). The magnitude ab sin(theta) stays the same, but the direction flips. This is a fundamental difference from the dot product which IS commutative.

student_says: cross product uses cos theta
a x b = ab cos theta
cross product formula has cosine
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: The cross product MAGNITUDE is ab sin(theta). The dot product uses cosine. Remember: cross product measures how much the vectors are TILTED relative to each other (sin measures tilt/rotation), while dot product measures how much they ALIGN (cos measures alignment). Maximum cross product is at 90° where sin = 1.

student_says: cross product is always perpendicular to both
a x b always perpendicular to a and b
cross product result lies in same plane
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: The cross product IS always perpendicular to BOTH original vectors — this is its defining feature. The result vector n points along the axis perpendicular to the plane containing a and b. This is why torque (r×F) makes an object spin around an axis perpendicular to both r and F.

student_says: cross product zero means perpendicular vectors
zero cross product means 90 degrees
a x b = 0 means perpendicular
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Cross product is ZERO when vectors are PARALLEL (theta = 0°) or ANTIPARALLEL (theta = 180°), because sin(0) = sin(180) = 0. It is MAXIMUM at 90°. This is the OPPOSITE of the dot product, which is zero at 90° and maximum at 0°/180°.

student_says: cross product result lies in same plane
a x b is in the plane of a and b
cross product doesn't leave the 2D plane
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: The cross product is defined only in 3D (and 7D). The result vector is perpendicular to the plane containing a and b. If a and b lie flat on a table, a×b shoots straight UP out of the table (or straight DOWN). It NEVER lies in the same plane.

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Projectile motion

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Gravity acts ONLY vertically (downward). There is NO horizontal force, so a_x = 0 and v_x = u cos(theta) stays CONSTANT throughout the entire flight. The horizontal motion is uniform. Only the vertical velocity changes: v_y = u sin(theta) - gt. Students confuse the slowing of the vertical component with the horizontal component.

object stops at top of trajectory
at maximum height v = 0
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: At the highest point, only the VERTICAL component v_y = 0. The HORIZONTAL component v_x = u cos(theta) is still there and unchanged. The velocity at the top is v = u cos(theta) — purely horizontal. The object never stops moving horizontally.

student_says: 45 degrees always gives maximum range
max range is always at 45 degrees
theta = 45 for max range always
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: theta = 45° gives maximum range ONLY when launch and landing heights are equal (level ground). If you launch from a height h above the landing point, the optimal angle is LESS than 45°. The range formula R = u² sin(2theta)/g only applies for level ground projection.

student_says: acceleration is zero at the top
no acceleration at highest point
g = 0 at maximum height
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Acceleration is ALWAYS -g (downward) throughout the entire trajectory, including at the highest point. Gravity never stops acting. At the top, velocity is purely horizontal but acceleration is still straight down. The path curves because velocity and acceleration are perpendicular at that instant.

student_says: speed is same at same height on way up and down
velocity is same at equal heights
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: The SPEED (magnitude of velocity) IS the same at equal heights on the way up and down (by symmetry of energy conservation). But the VELOCITY (vector) is NOT the same — the direction is different. At the same height on descent, the vertical component has opposite sign but same magnitude. The horizontal component is unchanged.

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Uniform circular motion

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Acceleration is the rate of change of VELOCITY, and velocity is a vector (magnitude AND direction). In UCM, speed is constant but direction changes continuously. Delta-v is non-zero because the velocity vector keeps turning, so there IS a real acceleration: a = v²/r directed toward the center. This is the centripetal acceleration.

student_says: centripetal force is a new type of force
there is a special centripetal force
centripetal force adds to other forces
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Centripetal force is NOT a new force — it is whatever REAL force (tension, friction, gravity, normal) happens to be pulling inward. It is the NET inward force required for circular motion. Saying 'centripetal force acts' is like saying 'net force acts' — it is a role played by existing forces, not a separate force.

student_says: centrifugal force is real
centrifugal force pushes outward
centrifugal balances centripetal
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Centrifugal force is a pseudo force observed ONLY in the rotating (non-inertial) frame. In the inertial frame, there is no outward force — the object wants to go straight (Newton's first law) and the centripetal force bends it into a circle. In the rotating frame, you FEEL pushed outward, but this is because your frame is accelerating.

student_says: angular speed and linear speed are same
omega and v are the same thing
omega = v always
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Linear speed v and angular speed omega are related by v = r*omega, but they are different quantities with different units. v is in m/s (distance per time); omega is in rad/s (angle per time). At a larger radius, the same angular speed gives a higher linear speed. They are proportional, not identical.

student_says: period and frequency are same
T = f
period equals frequency
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Period T and frequency f are reciprocals: T = 1/f and f = 1/T. They measure opposite things: T is time for ONE revolution, f is revolutions per unit time. If T = 2 seconds, then f = 0.5 Hz. They can never be equal (except at T = f = 1, which is a coincidence at T = 1 second).

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Newton's First Law (inertia, force, mass)

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Newton's First Law says the OPPOSITE: a body in uniform motion continues in uniform motion with NO force at all. In daily life, objects stop because friction (a force) acts against them. On a frictionless surface, a pushed object would never slow down. The force is needed to START motion or CHANGE it, not to maintain it.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Inertia is a PROPERTY of matter, not a force. It is the resistance to change in motion. You cannot 'apply' inertia or measure it with a force meter. Mass is the quantitative measure of inertia. More mass = more inertia = harder to change motion. But inertia itself is not a force.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: More mass means MORE inertia, not less. A heavier object is harder to start moving and harder to stop. Students sometimes confuse 'inertia' with 'ease of motion' and think light objects resist more. The correct relation: inertia is directly proportional to mass.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Inertia has TWO forms: static inertia (resistance to starting motion from rest) AND dynamic inertia (resistance to stopping or changing motion of a moving object). A moving car has inertia too — that is why it takes distance and braking force to stop it. Inertia is about resisting ANY change in motion.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Force is in the direction of ACCELERATION, not velocity. If you throw a ball upward, velocity is upward but force (gravity) is downward. entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Linear momentum (p = mv)

student_says: momentum is scalar

momentum magnitude only no direction

If a 2 kg object moves at 5 m/s east, its momentum is 10 kg m/s east — not just 10 kg m/s. Always state the direction. CISCE examiners (2025 PPA) noted many candidates 'lack clarity regarding vectors and scalars' and lost marks.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Momentum (p = mv) and KE (K = 1/2 mv^2) are completely different quantities. Momentum is a VECTOR (has direction), KE is a SCALAR. Momentum is conserved in ALL collisions; KE is only conserved in elastic collisions. A heavy slow truck and light fast bullet can have the same momentum but vastly different KE.

student_says: heavier object always has more momentum

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Momentum depends on BOTH mass AND velocity: p = mv. A small fast bullet can have more momentum than a slow truck. A 0.01 kg bullet at 800 m/s has p = 8 kg m/s. A 1000 kg truck at 0.01 m/s has p = 10 kg m/s — but a slightly slower truck (0.005 m/s) has LESS momentum than the bullet. Both factors matter.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Impulse is the CHANGE in momentum, not momentum itself: J = F_avg * delta_t = delta_p. Impulse has units of N·s (or kg·m/s — same as momentum). But impulse is what you APPLY (force over time), while momentum is what the object HAS. The impulse-momentum theorem says the impulse applied equals the change in momentum.

Force (N = kg m/s²) and momentum (kg m/s) are different quantities. Energy (Joule = N·m = kg m²/s²) is yet another different quantity.

For example, if you push a box to the right, static friction acts to the LEFT, opposing the tendency to move right.

Students often incorrectly take the full mg as acting along the slope or forget to resolve at all.

The direction depends on which way the block is (or tends to be) moving, not a fixed 'upward' direction.

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Centripetal force and banking of roads

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Centripetal force is a REAL force directed TOWARD the center of the circular path. 'Centrifugal force' is a PSEUDO-FORCE felt only in a rotating (non-inertial) frame of reference. It is NOT a real reaction to centripetal force. When a car turns, friction from the road pushes INWARD (centripetal) - there is no outward-pushing force. The feeling of being pushed outward is inertia resisting the change in direction. CISCE 2025 PPA (Question 2, high frequency) directly flagged this misconception.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Centripetal force is NOT a new type of force. It is whatever existing force (tension, friction, gravity, normal reaction) happens to be pointing toward the center of the circular path. For a satellite, it's gravity. For a ball on a string, it's tension. For a car on a flat road, it's friction. The name 'centripetal' describes the ROLE of the force (center-seeking), not its identity.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: A banked road is designed so that at a DESIGN SPEED (v = sqrt(R*g*tan(theta))), no friction is needed. At speeds LOWER than design speed, friction acts UP the bank. At speeds HIGHER than design speed, friction acts DOWN the bank. Only at exactly the design speed is friction zero. In practice, some friction is almost always involved.

The dot product of two vectors is always a SCALAR - a single number with a sign (+ or -) that indicates whether energy is transferred TO or FROM the body, NOT a direction in space. When you hold a box stationary against gravity, displacement is zero, so W = 0. When force is perpendicular to displacement (theta = 90 degrees), cos(90) = 0, so W = 0 (e.g., centripetal force in uniform circular motion does no work).

For a non-conservative force (friction), work depends on the actual path length. Students confuse these two scenarios.

entries.title: Work done by a variable force (integration)

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: The factor 1/2 is ESSENTIAL. The spring force grows linearly from 0 to kx as the spring is stretched from 0 to x. The AVERAGE force during the stretch is kx/2, not kx. Work = average force x displacement = (kx/2) * x = 1/2 * k * x^2. This is also the triangular area under the F-x graph (not a rectangle). Dropping the 1/2 doubles the energy, which is physically wrong. CISCE 2020 PPA noted candidates mishandling this basic algebra.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: W = F * S (or F * S * cos(theta)) is ONLY valid for CONSTANT force. When force varies with position, you cannot multiply a single F by total S. Instead, you must integrate: W = integral(F dx). Geometrically, this is the AREA under the F-x curve, not a simple rectangle. Integration is needed because each infinitesimal segment has a different force value.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Integration of F dx gives positive work when force and displacement are in the same direction, but NEGATIVE work when they are in opposite directions. The integral handles sign naturally - below the x-axis (force opposite to displacement), the area contributes negatively. For a spring being compressed vs stretched, the sign of work depends on whether the force assists or opposes the displacement.

It has nothing to do with 'saving' energy or being constant. Gravity and springs are conservative; friction is non-conservative because work done by friction depends on the path length (longer path = more energy lost). The key test: in a closed loop, does total work = 0?

When solving problems, if friction is present, use: KE_i + PE_i = KE_f + PE_f + (thermal energy lost).

A smaller bubble has a much sharper curvature, so the surface tension pulls inward much more tightly, creating HIGHER pressure inside. If a small bubble connects to a large bubble via a tube, air flows from the small bubble into the large one, making the small one shrink!

A candle flame in space is spherical and quickly suffocates because the hot CO2 doesn't rise.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: The defining feature of an isothermal process is that the temperature stays exactly CONSTANT (DeltaT = 0). While the gas does work (which would normally cool it), heat flows IN from the surroundings (the reservoir) to exactly compensate for the energy used in doing work. If a gas expands and does work, heat must flow IN (Q > 0) to prevent the gas from cooling. No heat exchange (Q = 0) is an adiabatic process.

entries.title: Adiabatic process

entries.title: Second law of thermodynamics

The Second Law only states that you cannot have COMPLETE (100%) conversion of heat into work in a cyclic process. Some heat must always be rejected to a colder sink. CISCE examiners note students confuse 'no perfect engine' with 'no engine'.

The heat rejected to the sink is still energy, it's just dispersed and can no longer be used to do work. Total energy is conserved, but 'useful' energy decreases.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: The entropy of a SPECIFIC SYSTEM can absolutely decrease (e.g., freezing water into ice, or cleaning your room). However, the Second Law states that the TOTAL entropy of the UNIVERSE (system + surroundings) must always increase. If a system's entropy decreases, it must release heat that increases the surroundings' entropy by an even larger amount.

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Carnot cycle and efficiency

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: No real OR ideal engine operating between two finite temperatures can reach 100% efficiency. Carnot efficiency (eta = 1 - T2/T1) equals 1 (or 100%) ONLY if the sink temperature T2 is 0 Kelvin, which is physically unattainable (Third Law of Thermodynamics). Even the 'perfect' Carnot engine must reject some heat.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: The Carnot engine is a purely theoretical, idealized construct. It assumes perfectly reversible processes, zero friction, and infinitely slow operations (to remain in thermal equilibrium). It cannot be built in reality. It serves as a theoretical maximum 'speed limit' for how efficient any real engine could possibly be.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Carnot's theorem explicitly states that the efficiency of a Carnot engine is INDEPENDENT of the working substance. It depends exclusively on the temperatures of the hot source (T1) and the cold sink (T2). Whether you use ideal gas, steam, or liquid, the maximum theoretical efficiency remains 1 - T2/T1.

Rotation about the bond axis itself (the line connecting the two atoms) has a negligible moment of inertia because the mass is concentrated almost entirely on that axis. In reality, it is mathematically essential for the differential equation. Without the minus sign, the equation represents exponential growth (like pushing something away faster and faster), not an oscillation. The minus sign creates the 'restoring' nature that brings the object back.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students think a vector is simply a signed number. This only works in one-dimensional problems (moving along a straight line). In 2D and 3D space, a simple sign is not enough to specify direction. A true vector needs components along multiple axes (like A = ai + bj + ck) to precisely describe 'which way' it points in space.

student_says: magnitude can be negative
magnitude is -5
length of vector is negative
magnitude negative ho sakta hai
absolute value nahi lena hai
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students confuse the scalar component of a vector with its magnitude. The magnitude represents the 'length' or 'size' of the vector and is calculated as the square root of the sum of the squares of its components: sqrt(a^2 + b^2 + c^2). Since squares are positive and the principal square root is positive, magnitude is always a positive number (or zero). It can never be negative.

student_says: unit vector has units of meters
unit vector has the same unit as the vector
unit vector ki unit kya hai
it is measured in meters per second
unit vector carries the dimension
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students assume that because it is called a 'unit' vector, it carries physical units. A unit vector (like i, j, k or n-cap) is dimensionless; its only job is to point in a specific direction. It is found by dividing a vector by its own magnitude (which cancels out the units). Its magnitude is exactly the pure number 1.

entries.title: Energy in SHM (kinetic and potential)

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students confuse the varying kinetic and potential energies with the total mechanical energy. In an ideal SHM, total mechanical energy (E = KE + PE) is strictly conserved and constant at all points (E = 1/2 m omega^2 A^2). Only the *distribution* between KE and PE changes as the object moves.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students confuse kinetic and potential energy locations. At the center (mean position), the restoring force has done all its work, the spring/pendulum is unstretched/at lowest height, so Potential Energy is zero. Because it is moving fastest here, Kinetic Energy is maximum.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students forget the squared relationship in the energy formula. Total energy is E = 1/2 m omega^2 A^2. It is proportional to the *square* of the amplitude. If you double the amplitude, the total energy increases by a factor of four, not two.

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Simple pendulum

classification_patterns.pattern: mass badhane se time period kya hoga

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students intuitively feel that a heavier object is harder to move and thus should swing slower. However, in the derivation of the pendulum's acceleration, mass cancels out (F = -mg*sin(theta) and a = F/m, so a = -g*sin(theta)). The time period T = 2*pi*sqrt(L/g) is completely independent of the bob's mass.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students forget that gravity provides the restoring force for a simple pendulum. In zero gravity (or free fall), g = 0. Looking at the formula T = 2*pi*sqrt(L/g), as g approaches 0, T approaches infinity. The pendulum will not swing; it will just float or stay where you put it.

amplitude badhane se T change hoga

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: For small angles (less than about 15 degrees), the simple pendulum executes SHM, and the time period is independent of amplitude (isochronism). Students often extrapolate from large angle swings (where this approximation breaks down) to small angles. For the standard SHM pendulum, amplitude does not affect T.

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Spring oscillator

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students mistakenly believe gravity affects the oscillation speed of a vertical spring. Gravity only pulls the mass down to a new equilibrium position (stretching it by mg/k). Once it oscillates around this *new* equilibrium, the net restoring force is still just -kx. The time period T = 2*pi*sqrt(m/k) remains exactly the same as a horizontal spring.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students confuse the properties of the attached object with the properties of the spring itself. The spring constant (k) is an inherent property of the spring (depending on its material, coil thickness, etc.). Changing the attached mass changes the time period, but the spring's stiffness (k) remains constant.

student_says: springs in series add like resistors

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students incorrectly apply the formula for electrical resistors in series to springs. For springs, connecting them in series makes the system *looser* (more stretch for the same force). The correct formula is 1/k_eq = 1/k1 + 1/k2. Springs in parallel add up directly (k_eq = k1 + k2) because they share the load.

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Wave motion and wave equation

classification_patterns.pattern: plus sign means wave travels right

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students intuitively associate a '+' sign with moving forward or to the right (positive x-direction). However, in the wave equation, to track a crest (constant phase), if time 't' increases, 'x' must *decrease* to keep (kx + wt) constant. Therefore, y = A sin(kx + wt) describes a wave moving to the *left* (-x direction). y = A sin(kx - wt) moves to the right.

student_says: wave equation is for one particle
it shows the path of a single atom
y is the path of the wave

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students confuse the wave profile with the trajectory of a single particle. The wave equation y(x,t) gives the displacement 'y' of *any* particle located at position 'x' at any time 't'. It represents the entire medium, not just one particle. A single particle just moves up and down (in a transverse wave), it doesn't move forward along the x-axis.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students confuse the symbol 'k' used in SHM (spring constant, N/m) with the 'k' used in the wave equation. In waves, 'k' is the angular wave number (k = 2*pi/lambda, measured in rad/m). It represents spatial frequency (how many waves per meter), not stiffness.

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Transverse and longitudinal waves

classification_patterns.pattern: transverse aur longitudinal mein confuse ho gaya

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students confuse the propagation of the wave (energy/disturbance) with the movement of the medium itself. In both transverse and longitudinal waves, particles only oscillate back and forth (or up and down) around their fixed mean positions. They do not travel bodily with the wave. CISCE examiners repeatedly flag this fundamental confusion.

student_says: sound is a transverse wave
light is longitudinal
sound waves have crests and troughs
sound travels like a rope wave

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students mix up the two primary examples of waves. Light (EM waves) is transverse (fields oscillate perpendicular to travel). Sound in air is longitudinal (air molecules oscillate parallel to travel, creating compressions and rarefactions, not crests and troughs).

student_says: longitudinal waves have crests and troughs

trough in longitudinal
longitudinal me bhi up down hota hai

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students apply transverse wave terminology to all waves because graphs of sound waves are often drawn as sine waves (where the y-axis is pressure or density, not physical height). Longitudinal waves physically consist of compressions (high density) and rarefactions (low density), not physical crests and troughs.

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Speed of wave motion and Newton's/Laplace's formula

classification_patterns.pattern: what is newtons formula for sound

student_says: pressure increases speed of sound
more pressure means faster sound
pressure badhane se speed badhegi

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students look at v = sqrt(gamma*P / rho) and assume increasing P increases v. However, at a constant temperature, Boyle's law states that volume decreases proportionally as pressure increases, meaning density (rho) increases exactly as much as P. The ratio P/rho remains constant. Therefore, a change in pressure alone (at constant temperature) has NO effect on the speed of sound.

student_says: newton assumed adiabatic process
newton used gamma
laplace assumed isothermal
newton said it was adiabatic
isothermal was laplace's idea
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students mix up the two theories. Newton incorrectly assumed the compressions and rarefactions happen slowly enough for heat to exchange, making it an *isothermal* process (temperature constant). Laplace corrected this by realizing sound travels too fast for heat exchange, so the process is *adiabatic* (requiring the inclusion of gamma, the ratio of specific heats).

student_says: speed of sound is independent of temperature
temperature doesn't change sound speed
temp se koi farq nahi padta
only medium matters not temp
formula me temp nahi hai
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students don't see 'T' directly in v = sqrt(gamma*P/rho) and assume temperature doesn't matter. But using the ideal gas law (P = rho*R*T/M), the formula becomes v = sqrt(gamma*R*T / M). The speed of sound is directly proportional to the square root of absolute temperature. Sound travels faster on a hot day.

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Principle of superposition and interference

classification_patterns.pattern: do waves bounce off each other

student_says: waves merge and lose identity

waves crash and combine permanently
they mix and don't separate
do wave milke ek ban jate hain
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students think waves interact like physical objects (like two clay balls sticking together). In reality, waves pass through each other completely unchanged. Superposition only describes the momentary resultant displacement *while* they overlap. After passing, each wave continues with its original amplitude, frequency, and direction.

student_says: destructive interference destroys energy

energy zero ho jati hai
cancellation means energy disappears
where does the energy go it vanishes
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students see the displacement become zero and assume energy is violated/destroyed. Energy is always conserved. In interference, energy is merely redistributed in space. The energy 'missing' from the regions of destructive interference (nodes) shows up in the regions of constructive interference (antinodes) where the amplitude is doubled (energy is 4x).

student_says: amplitudes always add up directly
just do A1 + A2
total amplitude is sum of amplitudes
hamesha add karna hai
resultant is always a1 + a2
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students forget about phase difference and just add scalar amplitudes. Superposition adds *displacements* (vectors/signed values), not amplitudes. If a crest (A) meets a trough (-A), the resultant displacement is 0, not 2A. The resultant amplitude depends entirely on the phase angle between them.

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Standing waves in strings

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students confuse progressive (traveling) waves with standing waves. A standing wave is the superposition of two identical waves traveling in opposite directions. The net energy transport is exactly zero. Energy stays localized in the loops between adjacent nodes, just oscillating between kinetic and potential forms without moving down the string.

student_says: nodes are maximum amplitude

node is the peak

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students mix up the terminology. 'Node' means 'no displacement' (zero amplitude) — these are the points that stay completely still. 'Antinode' means maximum displacement. A helpful mnemonic is 'Anti-node = Action, Node = Nothing'.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students struggle with the geometry of standing waves. A full wavelength (lambda) contains three nodes (e.g., start, middle, end). The distance between two consecutive nodes is lambda/2. The distance between a node and the very next antinode is half of that, which is lambda/4.

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Standing waves in organ pipes

classification_patterns.pattern: both ends are antinodes in closed pipe

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students generalize the rule for open pipes to all pipes. An open end allows air to move freely, creating a displacement antinode. A closed end physically blocks the air from moving, forcing a displacement node (zero movement). A closed pipe has a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end.

student_says: closed pipe has even harmonics

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students assume the harmonic series is always f, 2f, 3f... like in strings or open pipes. Because a closed pipe must always have a node at one end and an antinode at the other, it can only fit odd quarter-wavelengths (lambda/4, 3lambda/4, 5lambda/4). Thus, it only produces odd harmonics (f, 3f, 5f...). The 'even' harmonics physically cannot satisfy the boundary conditions.

student_says: open pipe formula is v/4L
fundamental of open is v/4L
open pipe ka v/4L hota hai

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students mix up the formulas for open and closed pipes. An open pipe fits half a wavelength (lambda/2) in its fundamental mode, so L = lambda/2, giving f = v/2L. A closed pipe fits a quarter wavelength (lambda/4), giving f = v/4L. Open pipes have the same formula structure as strings fixed at both ends.

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Beats

classification_patterns.pattern: beat frequency is the sum of frequencies
sum of frequency kyu nahi hota
can hear beats for any frequency

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students confuse the superposition of displacements (which do add together) with the resulting beat pattern. Beats are caused by the two waves drifting in and out of phase. The number of times they align (constructive interference) per second is exactly the *difference* in their frequencies, |f1 - f2|, because the faster wave gains exactly that many cycles per second on the slower one.

student_says: beats happen when amplitudes are different
different loudness causes beats
amplitude change hone se beats bante hain
need different intensities for beats
beats rely on amplitude difference
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students think beats are a phenomenon of varying amplitudes creating a new effect. In reality, beats require two waves of slightly different *frequencies*. If frequencies are identical but amplitudes differ, you just get a steady sound of a new constant amplitude. Beats are the periodic waxing and waning of sound caused by frequency mismatch.

student_says: can hear beats for any frequency difference
beats happen for 100hz difference
any two sounds make beats
we can hear beats if f1 - f2 is 50
no limit to beat frequency
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students apply the math blindly without considering human biology. While the math |f1 - f2| always works, human ears cannot distinguish beats if the frequency difference is more than about 10 Hz. Above 10 Hz, the beats are too fast, and the brain perceives them as a continuous rough sound or a separate tone, rather than individual pulses (waxing and waning).

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Electric charges (types and properties)

classification_patterns.pattern: charge create hota hai na rub karne se

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students violate the law of conservation of charge. Charge is never created or destroyed; it is only transferred. When you rub two objects, friction provides the energy to strip existing electrons from one material and move them to the other. The total net charge of the two-body system remains exactly zero.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students assume that to become positive, an object must gain positive particles (protons). In solid materials, protons are locked tightly in the atomic nucleus and do not move. An object becomes positively charged solely by *losing* negative electrons, leaving an excess of the stationary positive protons.

student_says: neutral means no charges inside

neutral body is empty of charge
usme koi charge nahi hota
neutral means charge is absent
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students confuse 'net charge of zero' with 'absence of charge'. A neutral object contains billions of charges; it just has exactly equal numbers of protons (positive) and electrons (negative), so their effects cancel out perfectly. It is full of charge, just balanced.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: CISCE examiners explicitly observe candidates failing to distinguish these two. Biot-Savart gives the differential magnetic field (dB) of a tiny current element and requires complex integration over the entire wire, making it suitable for ANY arbitrary geometry. VL leads the current by 90 degrees, and VC lags by 90 degrees, meaning they are 180 degrees out of phase with each other (they point in opposite directions). This net reactance is 90 degrees out of phase with the resistance R. Therefore, you must use the Pythagorean theorem to find the total impedance: Z = sqrt(R^2 + (XL - XC)^2).

Because they cancel each other out in the formula Z = sqrt(R^2 + (XL - XC)^2), the total impedance Z becomes equal to just R. This is the MINIMUM possible impedance, which means the current is actually at its MAXIMUM, not zero.

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Interference of light (principle)

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Sustained interference requires COHERENT sources, which means they must emit light with a constant phase difference. Two independent bulbs (or torches) are incoherent. Their atoms emit light randomly, so the phase difference changes millions of times per second (~10^-9 s). The interference pattern shifts so rapidly that our eyes just see a uniform average brightness, not fringes. CISCE 2023 examiners noted students severely lacked understanding of coherence.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Energy is never destroyed; it is only redistributed. In an interference pattern, the energy that is 'missing' from the dark fringes has simply shifted to the bright fringes. The average intensity across the whole screen remains exactly equal to the sum of the intensities of the two individual waves. This perfectly obeys the law of conservation of energy.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Coherent sources do NOT need to have a zero phase difference. They only need to have a CONSTANT phase difference with respect to time. It could be a constant 0, a constant 90 degrees, or a constant 180 degrees. As long as it doesn't fluctuate randomly, the sources are coherent and will produce a stable interference pattern.

A very bright red light might eject no electrons, while a dim blue light ejects fast ones.

Because light acts as a particle (photon), an electron absorbs a whole photon at once. If the photon has enough energy (f > f_threshold), the electron pops out immediately, even if the light is extremely dim.

Comparing this to y = mx + c, the slope 'm' is h/e, NOT h. To find Planck's constant (h), you must multiply the slope by the charge of an electron (e). misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Kinetic energy cannot be negative. If the incident photon energy (hf) is less than the work function (Φ), the equation K_max = hf - Φ would mathematically yield a negative number, but physically, this means NO emission takes place at all. The electron simply doesn't absorb enough energy to escape, so K_max is zero, not negative.

entries.title: Photon and photon momentum (p = h/lambda)

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students mistakenly apply classical mechanics (p = mv) to a relativistic quantum particle. A photon has zero REST mass, but it is never at rest; it always travels at the speed of light (c). Its momentum is derived from its energy via the relativistic relation E = pc (or E = hc/λ), which gives p = E/c = h/λ. It definitely carries momentum and can push things (radiation pressure).

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: The CISCE 2020 examiner noted candidates 'treated wavelengths as speed'. All photons in a vacuum travel at exactly the same speed: c (3 x 10^8 m/s), regardless of their wavelength or frequency. Wavelength (λ) determines the photon's energy and momentum (color, in the case of visible light), not its speed.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: While it is historically common to talk about 'relativistic mass' (m = E/c^2), modern physics prefers to say a photon strictly has NO mass (rest mass is exactly zero). It has energy and momentum. Assigning a 'moving mass' to a photon often confuses students into trying to use classical formulas like 1/2 mv^2. It's better to stick to E = hf and p = h/λ.

entries.title: Particle nature of light (dual nature)

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Light does NOT switch its identity or 'transform' back and forth. It is always a single, unified quantum entity (a photon/quantum wave) that naturally possesses both characteristics simultaneously. Which aspect you OBSERVE depends entirely on the macroscopic experimental setup (e.g., slits for waves, metal plates for particles). It's like a cylinder: look from the side, it's a rectangle; look from the top, it's a circle. The cylinder itself never changes shape.

Interference, diffraction, and polarization CANNOT be explained by particles; they strictly prove the WAVE nature of light. The photoelectric effect and Compton scattering CANNOT be explained by classical waves; they strictly prove the PARTICLE nature of light.

A 'particle' in quantum mechanics (a photon) just means the energy is QUANTIZED—it arrives in discrete, indivisible packets or chunks, rather than a continuous, smooth flow. It has no physical volume or solid boundary.

entries.title: Properties of air (no colour, can be felt)

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Children associate 'real' things with having color or being solid. Many real things are colorless, like pure water or clean glass. Air is just like clear glass -- it is there, but light passes right through it so we don't see a color.

entries.title: Day and night formation (through pictures)

entries.title: Directions (left/right, above/below, near/far)

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Objects that float and sink in water

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students generalize that material alone dictates sinking. While a solid block of iron sinks, iron shaped like a bowl (or a ship) traps air and displaces water, allowing it to float.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students confuse size with density. A huge iceberg or a massive plastic ball floats, while a tiny pebble sinks. Size alone does not determine if something will float.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students confuse the overall weight of an object with how heavy it is for its size (density). A ship is heavy overall, but it is hollow and full of air, making it light for its large size, which allows it to float like an upside-down empty bowl.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: While water provides the upward push (buoyancy), trapping air makes the overall object less dense than water. Without the trapped air spaces, the solid material (like iron) would be denser than water and would sink.

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Types of forces (muscular, gravitational, magnetic, frictional)

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Friction as a force

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students mistakenly believe that because friction is involved in movement (like walking), it pushes the object forward in the same direction. However, friction is a resistive force. It ALWAYS acts in the opposite direction to the motion (or intended motion). When you push a book right, friction pushes left to stop it.

student_says: friction only happens on rough surfaces

ice has zero friction

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students think smooth surfaces lack friction completely. While smooth surfaces have much less friction than rough ones, they still have some friction. If ice had zero friction, you could never even stand on it without slipping instantly, and an object sliding on it would never stop.

friction is like gravity

friction ground ka pull hai
friction holds us to the earth
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students confuse friction with gravity. Gravity pulls objects downwards towards the Earth. Friction acts parallel to the surfaces in contact, resisting sliding motion. Gravity keeps you on the floor; friction keeps you from sliding across it.

entries.subject: physics
entries.title: Uses and harmful effects of friction

classification_patterns.pattern: how does friction help us walk

friction ke sirf nuksan hain
