all four sides equal means square
this is too much to remember

student_says: square and rectangle are completely different
rectangle square nahi ho sakta
they have nothing in common
square is square, rectangle is rectangle
square aur rectangle same hote hain kya
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students fail to see the relationship between squares and rectangles. A square is actually a special kind of rectangle where all four sides are equal. Both have four straight sides and four corners.

student_says: triangle ulta hai toh kya hoga
if it points down it is not a triangle
triangle must point up
upside down triangle is wrong
that is a V shape not a triangle
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students believe a triangle must rest on a flat base and point upwards. They do not realize that rotating a shape does not change its identity. A triangle is any closed 2D shape with three straight sides.

student_says: a line is not a shape
line shape kaise ho sakti hai
line has no sides so it's not a shape
only closed things are shapes
straight line is just a drawing
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: At this introductory level, children often think only closed figures (like circles and squares) are shapes. A line is a basic 1D geometric figure, and in early geometry, it is introduced as a foundational element of shapes.

emotional_triggers: i don't understand sides and corners
this is too much to remember
why are there so many shapes

entries.subject: maths
entries.title: Length - introduction to vocabulary like near, far, thin, thick, longer/taller, shorter, high, low

classification_patterns.pattern: lamba aur mota same hai kya
kaise pata chalega kon far hai
give example of taller and shorter
is a building tall or long
what does frame of reference mean

student_says: the tree is far
the car is near
it is just far
kaise pata chalega kon far hai
far means far away from everything
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Children use distance words like 'near' and 'far' as absolute properties of an object, without stating the frame of reference (far from WHERE?). They need to learn that 'near' and 'far' depend on the observer's position.

student_says: lamba aur mota same hai kya
tall means thick
the fat tree is taller
thick and long are the same
if it is big it is thick and tall
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students confuse vertical height (tall/short) with width/girth (thick/thin). A tree can be short and thick, or tall and thin. They need to separate these two different dimensions of measurement.

student_says: near means small
small things are near
if it is far it is big
chota hai toh paas hoga
far away things look small so small means far
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Due to perspective, far objects look small, leading children to confuse the concept of distance with the concept of size. 'Near' describes distance, not how big or small the object actually is.

emotional_triggers: i always mix up thick and thin
why are there so many words
this is too hard to remember

entries.subject: maths
entries.title: Compare lengths of objects and arrange in order

classification_patterns.pattern: i don't align the starting ends
starting point same rakhna zaroori hai kya
it sticks out more so it is longer
how to order from shortest to longest
i don't get how to measure
put them on a straight line first
why push them against a book

student_says: it sticks out more so it is longer
starting point same rakhna zaroori hai kya
i just look at the top ends
one is pushed up so it is longer
i don't align the starting ends
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students compare objects without aligning their starting points. They declare an object longer just because its end sticks out further, ignoring that it might have started higher up. A fair comparison requires a shared baseline.

student_says: thicker means longer
the fat pencil is the longest
mota hai toh lamba hoga
it is bigger so it is longer
wide things are longer
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students judge length by the overall visual bulk or thickness of the object rather than its end-to-end dimension. They need to focus strictly on the linear distance from one end to the other.

student_says: i arranged them randomly
any order is fine
just put them next to each other
shortest longest samajh nahi aata order mein
middle one is longest
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: When asked to arrange objects in order (e.g., shortest to longest), students just place them side-by-side without applying a sorting rule. They need to learn the step-by-step process of finding the shortest, then the next, etc.

emotional_triggers: i don't get how to measure
i always get the order wrong

entries.subject: maths
entries.title: Measure short lengths using non-standard units (e.g. hand span)

classification_patterns.pattern: how to measure with hand span
hand span se kaise napte hain
what is a non standard unit
i leave gaps between my hands
why is my answer different from my friend
i don't understand how to measure
give example of non standard units
this hand span thing is hard
i just say a number without unit
must write hand spans after the number

student_says: the desk is 8
answer 8 aayega na
i just say the number
unit likhna bhool gaya
the answer is just a number
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students give only the numerical value without stating the unit. A measurement is meaningless without its unit (8 hand spans is very different from 8 finger widths). CISCE heavily penalizes answers without units.

student_says: i leave gaps between my hands
haath ke beech jagah chhod di
i overlap my hands
just put hands randomly
it doesn't have to touch exactly
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: When measuring with physical units like hand spans, students leave gaps between placements or overlap them. To get an accurate measurement, the unit must be laid end-to-end continuously without gaps or overlaps.

student_says: my friend got 6 and i got 8 so one is wrong
why is my answer different
meri reading alag kyu aayi
everyone should get the same number
hand span gives exact same answer for all
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students expect a standard, uniform answer. They do not realize that 'non-standard' units vary by person. A child's hand is smaller than an adult's, so it will take MORE child hand spans to measure the same desk.

emotional_triggers: i don't understand how to measure
this hand span thing is hard
why is my answer different from my friend
mera answer hamesha galat hota hai

entries.subject: maths
entries.title: Introduction to Zero through a subtraction pattern

classification_patterns.pattern: zero is not a real number
zero ka matlab kuch nahi na
zero subtract karne se kya hoga
i don't get what zero is
why do we even need zero

student_says: zero is not a real number
zero means no answer
zero number nahi hota
it is just empty not a number
you can't count zero so it's not a number
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students treat an empty result as 'no answer exists' rather than recognizing Zero as a genuine, mathematically valid number. Zero is the exact number that represents the count of an empty set.

student_says: 5 minus 0 is 0
if i take away zero it all disappears
zero subtract karne se zero aata hai
any number minus zero is zero
zero makes everything zero
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students confuse taking away zero (taking away nothing) with the result being zero. If you have 5 chocolates and you take away 0 (none), you still have 5 chocolates left, not 0.

student_says: zero means nothing so don't write it
leave it blank for zero
kuch nahi bacha toh likhna nahi hai
no need to write zero
blank space is zero
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Because zero represents 'nothing', students think they should leave the answer space blank. They must learn that zero has a specific symbol (0) that must be written to record the answer 'none'.

emotional_triggers: i don't get what zero is
why do we even need zero

entries.subject: maths
entries.title: Estimation of short distances and their verification using non-uniform units

classification_patterns.pattern: the estimate must be exactly correct
exact answer nahi aaya toh wrong hai na
guess aur measure mein kya farq hai
i guessed 6 and it was 7 so i failed
an estimate is a thoughtful guess

student_says: the estimate must be exactly correct
mera guess galat tha
exact answer nahi aaya toh wrong hai
i guessed 6 and it was 7 so i failed
if it is not the exact number it is a bad guess
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students treat an estimate like a standard math problem where there is only one right answer. They must learn that an estimate is a 'thoughtful guess'—if it is close to the actual measurement, it is a successful estimate.

student_says: i just said 100 hand spans
guess wildly without looking
any number is a guess
kuch bhi bol do guess hai
i don't need to look just say 50
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students confuse a 'thoughtful guess' with a 'wild guess'. Estimation requires looking at the object, visualizing the unit, and making a reasonable approximation, not just shouting a random large or small number.

student_says: i measure it first then write the guess
measure karke guess likh diya
how can i guess before measuring
guess is just writing the measurement again
i cheat and measure to get the guess right
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Because students fear being 'wrong', they measure the object first and then write that exact number as their 'estimate'. This defeats the purpose of the estimate-measure-compare cycle.

emotional_triggers: mera guess hamesha galat hota hai
i am scared to guess wrong
why can't i just measure it

entries.subject: maths
entries.title: Weight - compare heavy and light objects

classification_patterns.pattern: bada hai toh heavy hoga na
balance scale kaise kaam karta hai
heavy aur light samajh nahi aaya
if i can carry it, it must be light
how to use a toy balance
test me on heavy and light
the side that goes down is lighter
kaise pata chalega kon heavy hai
balance scale going down means heavy

student_says: bigger objects are always heavier
bada hai toh heavy hoga na
large means heavy
the big cotton ball is heavier than small iron
size makes it heavy
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students judge weight purely by visual appearance and size. They must learn that material matters: a large bag of cotton can be much lighter than a small iron weight.

student_says: the side that goes up is heavier
up means more weight
jo upar gaya wo heavy hai
balance scale going up means it is big and heavy
lighter side goes down
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students misinterpret how a balance scale works. They associate 'up' with 'more' or 'bigger'. They need to understand that gravity pulls the heavier object down, pushing the lighter object up.

student_says: if i can carry it, it must be light
i can lift it so it's not heavy
heavy means nobody can lift it
main utha sakta hu matlab light hai
only cars and elephants are heavy
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students think 'heavy' and 'light' are absolute terms based on human strength. In math, heavy and light are comparative terms: a book is heavy compared to a pencil, even though a child can easily carry both.

emotional_triggers: heavy aur light samajh nahi aaya
i always guess the wrong one

entries.subject: maths
entries.title: Volume (Capacity) - order different containers in terms of their capacity

classification_patterns.pattern: a taller container always holds more
lamba glass zyada paani rakhta hai na
kaunsa bartan bada hai kaise pata chalega
capacity is how heavy it is
how to order containers by volume
i don't get this water pouring thing
does bucket hold more than cup
capacity means how much it can hold
how to measure capacity at home

student_says: a taller container always holds more
lamba glass zyada paani rakhta hai
tall means more capacity
it is higher so it holds more
short bowl holds less than tall thin glass
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students judge capacity by height alone, ignoring the width of the container. A short, wide bowl can hold more water than a tall, thin test tube. They must learn to measure rather than just look at height.

student_says: capacity is how heavy it is
heavy bottle has more capacity
bhaari hai toh capacity zyada hai
if the glass is heavy it holds more
weight and volume are same
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students confuse the weight of the material (e.g., a thick heavy glass mug) with its internal capacity. A light plastic bucket holds much more water than a heavy solid glass paperweight.

student_says: wide container holds less because water looks lower
paani neeche hai toh kam hai
the water didn't go high so it's less
level is low so volume is low
tall glass water is higher so it's more
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: When water is poured from a tall glass into a wide bowl, the water level drops. Students mistakenly think the amount of water has decreased, failing to grasp the conservation of volume.

emotional_triggers: i don't get this water pouring thing
why does the water look different

entries.subject: maths
entries.title: Time - distinguish between events using vocabulary like earlier-later

classification_patterns.pattern: earlier matlab chota hota hai kya
earlier aur later mein confuse ho gaya
pehle kya hua baad mein kya hua samajh nahi aata
how to know which is later
is waking up earlier than school

student_says: earlier means smaller
earlier matlab chota hota hai
less important things are earlier
small events are earlier
earlier is tiny
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students confuse the sequence of time with physical size or importance. 'Earlier' only refers to an event happening before another event on the timeline, regardless of how big or important the event is.

student_says: later means tomorrow
later is next day
later matlab kal
if it is today it cannot be later
later happens at night
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students associate 'later' strictly with the distant future (like tomorrow or night time) rather than understanding it is a relative term. 10:05 AM is 'later' than 10:00 AM.

student_says: school is earlier than breakfast
i sleep earlier than i play
pehle school phir uthna
events can happen in any order
lunch is earlier than morning
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students lack a mental timeline of their daily routine, causing them to mix up the logical chronological order of everyday events.

emotional_triggers: earlier aur later mein confuse ho gaya
pehle kya hua baad mein kya hua samajh nahi aata
i always mix up earlier and later

entries.subject: maths
entries.title: Time - differentiate between events of short and long duration

classification_patterns.pattern: how to know if event is long
short time aur long time samjhao
small biscuit means short event right
this time concept is too hard
test me on short and long time
playing is short because it is fun
i gave wrong answer for duration

student_says: small biscuit is short event
big meal is long because it is big
short means small size
big objects take long time
chota saman matlab short time
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students confuse physical size (small/big) with time duration (short/long). They think eating a small biscuit is 'short' because the biscuit is small, not because it takes less time. Time duration is about how long an action takes from start to finish, regardless of the object's size.

student_says: playing is short because it finishes fast
school is long because it is boring
fun things are short
khelna short time hota hai
watching movie is short
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students judge time based on psychological perception rather than actual duration. Fun activities feel like they end quickly, so students classify them as 'short duration', while boring activities feel 'long'. Playing for 2 hours is actually a long duration compared to brushing teeth for 2 minutes.

student_says: running is short because you go fast
walking is long
fast means short time
tez bhagna short time hai
slow means long duration
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students confuse speed (fast/slow) with duration (short/long). Running a marathon takes a long time even though you are moving fast, while taking one slow step takes a short time. Duration measures the total time spent, not the speed of the action.

emotional_triggers: samajh nahi aa raha short long

entries.subject: maths
entries.title: Time - verbal description of the sequence of events happening in a day

classification_patterns.pattern: i woke up next i slept
i don't know what comes next
this order thing is too hard
i keep messing up the order

next i went to school and later brushed teeth
i sleep first then eat dinner
pehle khana khaya phir utha
school ke baad brush kiya
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students use the sequence words (first, then, next) correctly in a sentence structure, but apply them to a completely illogical sequence of real-world events. They fail to mentally simulate the actual order in which daily activities must happen (e.g., you must wake up before you can eat breakfast).

student_says: night comes before evening
afternoon is before morning
evening is in the morning
raat pehle aati hai shaam se
morning then night then afternoon
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students confuse the vocabulary for the parts of the day. They do not understand the chronological progression of the sun (Morning -> Afternoon -> Evening -> Night) and mix up the labels.

student_says: first next then first
later then next first
i do first then first
sab sequence word ek saath
next next next
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students do not understand that sequence words represent a progression of time. They treat them as interchangeable filler words and string them together without attaching them to specific events in an ordered timeline.

emotional_triggers: mera order hamesha galat hota hai

entries.subject: maths
entries.title: Collection, representation and interpretation of simple information presented in a visual or by actual measurement

classification_patterns.pattern: i can just guess without counting
this group looks bigger so it is more
i am confused by the table
this is too boring and hard

student_says: i can just guess which is most
this group looks bigger
spread out group has more
dekh ke pata chal raha hai
bina count kiye bata dunga
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students rely on visual estimation instead of actual counting. A group of 3 items spread far apart can visually appear larger than a tight cluster of 5 items. Visual guessing is unreliable; data collection requires systematic counting and recording.

student_says: the big apples are more
taller stack has more toys
bada wala group jyada hai
large items mean bigger number
elephant group is more than ant group
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students confuse the physical size of the items with the quantity of items. Two elephants look massive compared to ten ants, but 10 is a larger quantity than 2. Data counting asks 'how many', not 'how big'.

student_says: i counted some twice
i forgot which ones i counted
just point anywhere to count
ginti bhool gaya beech mein
mix karke count karunga
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students count randomly without a system (like crossing out items or moving them as they count). This leads to double-counting or skipping items entirely, resulting in incorrect data representation.

emotional_triggers: i always get the count wrong
mera answer match nahi kar raha
i don't get this visual stuff

entries.subject: maths
entries.title: Simple patterns in shapes and numbers in the surroundings - their observation and extension

classification_patterns.pattern: last shape is triangle so next is triangle
i just repeat the last thing
i hate finding what comes next
kuch bhi likh do pattern mein
i got the next shape wrong

student_says: next is triangle because triangle is last
just repeat the last shape
jo aakhir mein hai wahi aayega
circle ke baad circle aayega
last item repeats
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students look only at the very last item in the sequence and assume it just repeats itself, rather than looking at the entire sequence to find the repeating unit (the 'rule'). In a triangle-circle-triangle-circle pattern, a triangle is followed by a circle, not another triangle.

student_says: red circle and blue circle are same
big square small square no difference
color doesn't matter in pattern
sirf shape dekhna hai color nahi
all triangles are same
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students ignore secondary attributes like size or color and only focus on the base shape. If the pattern is Red Circle, Blue Circle, Red Circle... the next must be Blue Circle, not just any circle. A pattern's rule includes all specific attributes of the items.

student_says: i can put any shape next
pattern means drawing shapes
kuch bhi draw kar do
next is star because i like stars
no rule just shapes
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students do not understand that a pattern is defined by a strict repeating rule. They view it merely as a collection of random shapes and think they can continue it with whatever shape they prefer.

emotional_triggers: dimaag kharab ho raha hai pattern mein
i don't get what comes next

entries.subject: maths
entries.title: Patterns from daily life experiences

classification_patterns.pattern: any group of pretty things is pattern
how to find pattern in real life
give example of pattern at home
pile of flowers is a pattern
i can't find patterns in my room
i don't get what a rule is
kuch bhi sundar cheez pattern hai

student_says: any group of pretty things is pattern
pile of colorful flowers is pattern
messy toys are a pattern because they look nice
sundar cheez pattern hoti hai
random colors are a pattern
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students confuse aesthetic appeal (things looking pretty together) with a mathematical pattern. A pattern requires a specific rule and a repeating unit in a fixed order. A random pile of flowers has no fixed order, so it is not a pattern.

student_says: a butterfly is a pattern
my face is a pattern
mirror image is a pattern
dono side same hai toh pattern hai
symmetrical things are patterns
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students confuse symmetry (where two sides mirror each other) with a repeating sequence. While symmetry is a mathematical concept, a repeating sequence pattern requires a unit that repeats sequentially (e.g., A-B-A-B), not just a single object that is mirrored.

student_says: it stops so it is not a pattern
pattern never ends
if it has 4 tiles it is not a pattern
pattern hamesha chalta rehta hai
short things can't be patterns
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students believe a pattern must go on forever. In reality, a pattern can be finite (like the stripes on a single shirt or the tiles on a small tabletop) as long as it demonstrates a repeating rule within that limited space.

emotional_triggers: mujhe samajh nahi aa raha life patterns

entries.subject: maths
entries.title: Counting objects from 1 to 99 by making groups leading to tens and ones

classification_patterns.pattern: counting 1 by 1 is the only way
there is no faster way to count
what is a bundle of ten
ten bundle is just one thing
make groups of ten to count fast

student_says: counting means saying one two three up to the number
there is no faster way to count
ek ek karke ginna padega
i have to count every single stick
grouping doesn't help me count
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students believe counting must always be done sequentially by ones (1, 2, 3... 23). They don't realize that grouping into bundles of ten allows for much faster and more accurate counting (10, 20, 21, 22, 23).

student_says: a bundle of ten is just one
if i have 2 bundles it means 2 sticks
bundle ko 1 ginte hain
ten sticks tied up becomes number 1
tens are just ones
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: When sticks are bundled, students lose the concept of the quantity inside. They count 2 bundles and 3 loose sticks as '5' total items, rather than understanding that 2 bundles represent 20.

student_says: twenty eight, twenty nine, twenty ten
thirty nine, thirty ten
after 29 comes 2010
twenty ten is a number
i don't know what comes after twenty nine
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students apply the 1-9 sequence blindly to the ones place without understanding that reaching 10 ones creates a new 'ten' group. So after 29, they say 'twenty-ten' instead of forming a new ten bundle to make thirty.

emotional_triggers: why do i have to group them
mera answer hamesha galat hota hai

entries.subject: maths
entries.title: Representing a number in groups of tens and ones

classification_patterns.pattern: digit 2 in 27 is same as 2 in 52
test me on tens and ones
this place value is too hard
left side is tens right is ones
i put the digits in wrong place

student_says: the digit 2 in 27 just means two
2 in 27 is same as 2 in 52
place doesn't change the number
dono jagah 2 ka matlab 2 hai
a 5 is always a 5
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students believe a digit holds an absolute value regardless of its position. They don't understand that place value changes the quantity a digit represents. In 27, the 2 means 'twenty' (two tens), but in 52, the 2 means 'two' (two ones).

student_says: 27 has 7 tens and 2 ones
first number is ones
right side is tens
ulta likh diya
tens are on the right
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students mix up the left-to-right convention of place value. They assign the tens value to the ones digit and vice versa, often reading right-to-left instead of left-to-right.

student_says: twenty seven is 207
thirty five is 305
write twenty then write seven
20 aur 7 mila ke 207
write 20 then 7 next to it
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students write numbers exactly as they hear them sequentially. They hear 'twenty' and write 20, then hear 'seven' and write 7, combining them into 207 instead of understanding that the 2 in the tens place already represents the twenty.

emotional_triggers: i hate writing tens and ones
mera number hamesha galat hota hai

entries.subject: maths
entries.title: Numeral and number names up to 99

classification_patterns.pattern: fifteen and fifty same hai kya
i wrote four five instead of forty five

student_says: 45 is read as four five
72 is seven two
just say the digits
alag alag digit bolna hai
read it like a phone number
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students read two-digit numbers by simply naming each digit individually from left to right, rather than using the proper place-value based number name. 45 is 'forty-five', representing four tens and five ones, not just a 4 and a 5.

student_says: fifty is fifteen
13 is thirty
teen and ty are the same
fifteen aur fifty mein confusion hai
14 is forty
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students confuse the '-teen' suffix (which means +10) with the '-ty' suffix (which means groups of 10). They write 15 when asked for fifty, or read 30 as thirteen. This is a very common phonetic and conceptual confusion.

student_says: forty and five
sixty and two
beech mein and likhna hai
twenty and eight
thirty plus one
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students insert the word 'and' between the tens and ones words. While common in spoken English in some regions, standard mathematical number names for two-digit numbers do not use 'and' (it is 'forty-five', not 'forty and five').

emotional_triggers: why is it not spelled fourty
mera spelling hamesha galat hota hai
i give up on number names

entries.subject: maths
entries.title: Comparison of numbers up to 99

classification_patterns.pattern: bigger ones digit means bigger number
49 is bigger than 56 because 9 is bigger
chota bada number kaise pata kare
i don't know which is greater
test me on greater than less than
i compared ones first by mistake

student_says: 49 is bigger than 56 because 9 is bigger than 6
bigger ones digit is always bigger
look at the last number to see which is big
jiska end bada wo number bada
9 is the biggest number so 29 is bigger than 41
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students mistakenly compare the ones digits instead of the tens digits. They see a 9 and immediately assume that number is larger, ignoring place value. The tens digit carries much more weight; 4 tens is always less than 5 tens, regardless of the ones.

student_says: seventeen is bigger than forty because the word is long
long spelling means big number
bada word matlab bada number
eighteen > twenty because it sounds longer
more letters means more value
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students use the length of the spoken or written word to judge numerical value. 'Seventeen' has more letters than 'forty', so they assume it represents a larger quantity.

student_says: 10 is bigger than 12 because of zero
zero makes numbers huge
zero add karne se bada hota hai
20 is bigger than 25
numbers with zero win
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students misapply the rule that 'adding a zero to the end multiplies by 10' and overgeneralize it to mean that any number ending in 0 is inherently very large, even larger than numbers with higher ones digits in the same ten.

emotional_triggers: i don't get which is bigger
mera greater than hamesha galat hota hai

entries.subject: maths
entries.title: Forming two digit numbers using the given digits (with or without repetition)

classification_patterns.pattern: how to make two digit number
what happens if i swap digits
add the digits to make a number
i can only make one number
i am confused by number forming
this digit swapping is too hard

student_says: 06 is a two digit number
put zero first to make a number
05 has two symbols so it is two digits
zero pehle laga sakte hain
0 and 8 makes 08
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students treat zero as a regular digit that can start a number. A two-digit number must have a non-zero digit in the tens place, because a leading zero has no value (06 is just 6, which is a one-digit number).

student_says: 3 and 7 makes 10
add them to form a number
plus karna hai dono ko
2 and 4 makes 6
combine means add
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: When asked to 'form a number using digits 3 and 7', students misunderstand the instruction and perform addition (3+7=10) instead of placing the digits in place value slots to make 37 or 73.

student_says: you can only make one number
3 and 7 only makes 37
no other number is possible
bas ek hi banega
swapping doesn't change it
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students do not realize that digits can be swapped between the tens and ones places to create different numbers. They lock the digits into the order they were presented.

emotional_triggers: i don't get how to make numbers
mera number form nahi ho raha

entries.subject: maths
entries.title: Sequences of numbers up to 99 in an increasing or decreasing order

classification_patterns.pattern: chota bada number kaise arrange kare
always look at tens digit first

student_says: compare the ones digit first
look at ones first
39 is bigger than 41 because 9 is big
last number decide karta hai
sort by the second digit
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students jump to compare the ones digit instead of the tens digit when ordering numbers. They see the 9 in 39 and the 1 in 41 and incorrectly place 39 as the larger number. The tens digit must always be evaluated first.

student_says: decreasing means getting bigger
ascending is going down
increasing means small
ghatna matlab badhna
decreasing starts with small number
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students confuse the vocabulary of ordering. They understand how to sort numbers but apply the wrong label, sorting largest to smallest when asked for increasing order.

student_says: i mix up the < and > signs
arrow points to big number
sign ulta laga diya
i don't know which way the mouth opens
less than sign is >
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: While sorting, students use the wrong inequality symbol to connect the sequence, writing 12 > 24 > 36 even though they intend to show increasing order. They forget that the open 'mouth' always faces the larger number.

emotional_triggers: mera sequence hamesha ulta hota hai

entries.subject: maths
entries.title: Before, after and in between numbers

classification_patterns.pattern: i am confused by before and after
this number line is too hard
i counted forward instead of backward

student_says: the number before 47 is 48
before means go forward
47 ke pehle 48 aata hai
after 20 is 19
before means next
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students confuse the spatial/temporal meaning of 'before' and 'after'. They move forward (add one) when asked for 'before', and move backward (subtract one) when asked for 'after'.

student_says: in between 5 and 7 is 12
add them to find between
beech wala number matlab plus karo
between 10 and 12 is 22
mix them together
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students do not understand 'in between' as a position on the number line. They treat the two given numbers as a prompt to perform an operation, usually addition, rather than finding the missing sequential number.

student_says: left is more
going back makes it bigger
number line ulta hota hai
smaller numbers are on the right
backward means bigger
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students overlook the standard direction of a number line (increasing left-to-right). They fail to mark the correct neighbour because they believe moving left increases the value.

emotional_triggers: i don't get before and after
i hate finding the middle number
mera before hamesha after hota hai

entries.subject: maths
entries.title: Numbers up to 99 and their number names

student_says: spelling is fourty
fourty likhna hai
it has a u because four has a u
fourty five
f-o-u-r-t-y
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Children see 'four' (4) and 'fourteen' (14) and wrongly assume 'forty' (40) must also contain a 'u'. 'Forty' is an irregular spelling that drops the 'u' completely.

student_says: spelling is ninty
n-i-n-t-y
drop the e in ninety
ninty likhna hai
ninty nine
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Unlike 'forty' which drops a letter, 'ninety' keeps the 'e' from 'nine'. Students over-apply spelling rules or guess phonetically, writing 'ninty' instead of 'ninety'.

student_says: sixteen is 60
seventy is 17
ty and teen are same
eighteen means 80
seventy is seventeen
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students confuse the phonetic endings '-teen' (meaning +10) and '-ty' (meaning groups of 10). They write the numeral 60 when asked for sixteen, or write the word 'seventy' when seeing 17.

emotional_triggers: why is english so confusing in math
mera marks spelling mein cut gaya

entries.subject: maths
entries.title: Construction of problems that can be solved by addition and subtraction of two digit numbers

classification_patterns.pattern: no need for a question at the end
i don't know how to write stories
this making story is too hard
more means add left means subtract

student_says: any two numbers can be added or subtracted
operation doesn't matter
kuch bhi add kar do
just put numbers together
plus or minus is same thing
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students believe the numbers themselves are all that matter, ignoring the context of the story. They don't realize that words like 'more', 'altogether', or 'left' dictate specific mathematical operations (addition or subtraction).

student_says: i had 5 apples and got 3 more. done.
no need to ask a question
story is enough
bas statement likh diya
question kyu puchna hai
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students write a situation but fail to include the question that requires solving. A math word problem must end with a question like 'How many are there in all?' to be complete.

student_says: 5 apples 3 bananas is 8 cars
just write numbers no story
5 plus 3 is a story
no need for words
bas number likh do
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students fail to construct a logical narrative. They either just write an equation (5+3=8) and call it a word problem, or they mix up units illogically (adding apples and bananas to get cars).

emotional_triggers: i don't know how to write stories

entries.subject: maths
entries.title: Estimation of the sum and difference between two given numbers

classification_patterns.pattern: round the answer not the numbers
rounding to nearest ten confusing hai

student_says: estimate must be exactly equal
i just calculated the real answer
estimate exact hona chahiye
approximate is wrong
why guess if i can calculate
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students confuse estimation with exact calculation. They believe an estimate is incorrect if it doesn't match the exact sum. They fail to understand that estimation is a tool for finding a quick, 'rough' answer.

student_says: 38 rounds to 30
always go down to the zero
just drop the ones digit
hamesha chota number lena hai
rounding means making it smaller
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students don't understand the midpoint rule of rounding (5 and up rounds up). They simply truncate the ones digit, turning 38 into 30 instead of rounding to the nearest ten, which is 40.

student_says: add first then round
round the final answer
pehle plus karo phir round karo
find exact sum then make it end in zero
38+23=61 then round 61 to 60
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: While mathematically giving a similar result sometimes, this defeats the purpose of estimation. Estimation is meant to make the addition process itself easier by rounding the components *before* adding (40+20=60), not doing the hard math first and rounding later.

emotional_triggers: i don't get why we estimate
why is my exact answer wrong
mera estimate hamesha galat hota hai

entries.subject: maths
entries.title: Construction of multiplication tables of 2, 3, 4, 5 through repeated addition and skip counting

classification_patterns.pattern: i just add any numbers for multiplication
multiplication table yaad nahi ho raha
why do we add the same number
ask me a question on table of 2
give me a hint for 3 times 4
how to jump on number line for 3s

student_says: table of 3 is 3 plus 4 plus 5
add any number to make table
i added 3 and 5 for the table
multiplication is adding different numbers
table banane ke liye alag number add karte hain
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students think multiplication is just adding any random numbers together. In reality, multiplication is repeated addition of the EXACT SAME number. The table of 3 means adding 3 every single time (3+3+3), representing equal groups.

student_says: skip count of 2 starts at 4
first jump is to 4
skip the first number
table of 5 starts at 10
pehle number ko chhod kar count karo
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students misunderstand 'skip counting' as literally skipping the first multiple. They start at the second multiple (e.g., 4 for the 2s table). Skip counting means jumping by a certain amount starting from 0, so the first landing spot is the number itself (0 + 2 = 2).

student_says: 2 times 3 is 5
3 times 4 is 7
multiply means add the two numbers
4 times 2 is 6
multiply karne bola toh add kar diya
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students confuse the multiplication symbol (x) with the addition symbol (+), or simply add the two factors together instead of making equal groups. 2 times 3 means two groups of 3 (which is 6), not 2 + 3.

entries.subject: maths
entries.title: Various situations on equal grouping and equal sharing that lead to repeated subtraction

classification_patterns.pattern: sharing and grouping are exactly same
yeh grouping samajh nahi aa raha
how many times do i subtract

student_says: sharing and grouping are the same thing
no difference between sharing and grouping
both are just subtracting so they are equal
sharing grouping ek hi baat hai
it doesn't matter if it's sharing or grouping
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: While both use repeated subtraction, the real-world meaning is different. In equal sharing, you know the NUMBER of groups (e.g., 3 friends) and want to find how many in each group. In equal grouping, you know the SIZE of each group (e.g., 4 toffees per bag) and want to find how many bags.

student_says: subtract until you get to 1
stop when 1 is left
repeated subtraction ends at 1
keep subtracting till 1
last mein 1 bacha chahiye
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students mistakenly stop subtracting when they reach 1, perhaps confusing it with counting. In equal grouping/sharing, you must subtract until your hand is completely empty, which means you stop when you reach 0.

student_says: subtract 3 then subtract 2
take away different numbers
just keep subtracting any number
sharing means giving anyone anything
alag alag number subtract karna hai
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students fail to grasp the 'equal' part of equal sharing/grouping. They subtract arbitrary amounts. Repeated subtraction for division requires subtracting the EXACT SAME amount every single time until you reach zero.

emotional_triggers: mujhe nahi samajh aa raha kab rukna hai
i always get the groups wrong

entries.subject: maths
entries.title: Mental addition and subtraction of two digit numbers

classification_patterns.pattern: how to add in my head
how to add tens and ones
i just put the numbers together
i forget the carry over in my mind
why do we split into tens and ones

student_says: write the tens and then write the ones
60 and 11 makes 611
just put the answers next to each other
tens add karke ones uske aage likh do
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: When the ones add up to more than 10 (like 6+5=11), students simply write the sum of the tens (60) and the sum of the ones (11) next to each other, creating a 3 or 4 digit number. They fail to mentally regroup the 11 into 1 ten and 1 one, which should make it 60 + 10 + 1 = 71.

student_says: i just dropped the extra 10
60 and 11 is 61
ignore the carry in mind
carry over dimaag mein bhool gaya
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Because they are doing it mentally, students forget to hold the carried 'ten' in their working memory. They add the ones (6+5=11), keep the 1, but forget to add the extra 10 to their tens total, resulting in 61 instead of 71.

student_says: add the 4 to the 5
add tens from one number to ones from other
mix the tens and ones
46 + 25 means 4+5 and 6+2
cross add kar diya
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students lose track of place value without the visual alignment of paper. They might add the tens digit of the first number to the ones digit of the second number. Mental math requires strictly grouping 'tens with tens' and 'ones with ones'.

emotional_triggers: i can't do it in my head
this is too confusing to remember

entries.subject: maths
entries.title: Creation of 2D-shapes through paper folding and paper cutting

classification_patterns.pattern: how to make shapes with paper
a fold is just a bend not a line
cut shapes are not real shapes
paper fold karke shape kaise banega
freehand drawing is better than folding
can i make a circle by folding

student_says: a fold is just a bend in the paper
the fold is not a real edge
crease is not a straight line
i have to draw it with a pencil to make an edge
fold karne se edge thodi banta hai
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students think a fold is just a physical bend and doesn't count as a geometric line or edge. In reality, when a fold is pressed flat, the crease forms a perfectly straight line that acts exactly like the straight edge of a 2D shape.

student_says: cut paper is not a real math shape
shapes are only drawn on paper
paper shapes don't count
real shapes are in the book
kaat ke banaya hua shape math ka nahi hai
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students restrict their idea of 'shapes' to ink printed on a page. A 2D shape is any flat closed boundary, whether drawn, cut out of paper, or formed by shadows. A paper cutout is a perfect physical model of a 2D shape.

student_says: i can just draw it freehand
my freehand line is straight enough
why fold when i can draw
drawing is better than folding for straight lines
haath se seedha line ban jayega
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Young students often fail to recognize that folding produces a reliably straight edge, whereas freehand drawing almost always produces a wobbly, non-straight line. The fold guarantees straightness.

emotional_triggers: i don't get how a fold is a line

entries.subject: maths
entries.title: Attribute of 2D shapes and their sides and corners

classification_patterns.pattern: how many sides does a circle have
corners are only at the top
how many corners in a rectangle
i keep mixing up sides and corners
example of corners in real life
circle me corner nahi hota na
mujhe corners count karna nahi aata

student_says: a circle has one side
the round edge is a side
circle ka ek side hota hai
it has one continuous side
the boundary of circle is its side
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: In geometry, a 'side' is defined as a STRAIGHT line segment that forms part of a polygon's boundary. A circle's boundary is a continuous curve, not a straight line. Therefore, a circle has 0 sides and 0 corners.

student_says: corners are only at the top
the bottom ones are not corners
triangle has 1 corner at the top
sirf upar wale ko corner bolte hain
corner means the peak
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students confuse the everyday meaning of 'corner' or 'peak' with the geometric vertex. A corner (vertex) is ANY point where two straight sides meet, regardless of whether it is at the top, bottom, or side of the shape.

student_says: sides can be curved
a heart has two curved sides
moon shape has curved sides
side gol bhi ho sakta hai
oval has curved sides
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students use the word 'side' loosely to mean any edge or boundary. In basic 2D shape attributes, a 'side' strictly means a straight line segment. Curved boundaries are just called curves or curved edges, not 'sides'.

emotional_triggers: i always count the sides wrong
i don't get what a corner is

entries.subject: maths
entries.title: Straight lines and representing them by paper folding, straightedge objects, stretched strings

classification_patterns.pattern: how to make straight line with string
any line with ruler is straight
how to fold paper for straight line
string has to be thick to be a line
yeh straight line samajh nahi aa raha
can a stretched thread be a line
i can't draw a straight line
loose string is a straight line
how many ways to represent straight line

student_says: any line drawn with a ruler is straight
if i use a scale it is automatically straight
ruler means straight line
scale se banaya toh straight hi hoga
even if my pencil slipped it's straight because of ruler
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students assume the tool (ruler) magically guarantees a straight line, ignoring the process. If the pencil slips, or the ruler moves while drawing, the resulting line is wobbly and NOT straight. A straight line is defined by its lack of bend, not by the tool used to attempt it.

student_says: freehand line is automatically not straight
you can't make a straight line without a ruler
haath se straight line nahi ban sakti
if i didn't use a scale it's not straight
only ruler makes straight lines
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: While it is difficult, a very careful freehand line can be nearly perfectly straight, and an edge (like a folded paper) can be used without a traditional ruler. The definition of a straight line is that it doesn't bend, regardless of how it was created.

student_says: any string is a straight line
a loose thread is a straight line
string ko zameen par rakh do toh straight line hai
just dropping a string makes a line
a curved string is still a straight line because it's string
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: A string only represents a straight line when it is stretched TIGHTLY between two points. If it is loose, sagging, or curved on the floor, it represents a curved line, not a straight one.

emotional_triggers: i can't hold the ruler still
why does it have to be perfect

entries.subject: maths
entries.title: Draw horizontal, vertical and straight lines

classification_patterns.pattern: horizontal and vertical are different types of lines
i mix up horizontal and vertical
mujhe lines samajh nahi aa rahi
how to remember vertical and horizontal
these line names are too hard
difference between standing and sleeping line

student_says: horizontal and vertical are different types of lines
a vertical line is not a straight line
they are two completely different things
horizontal alag line hai vertical alag
one is straight the other is vertical
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students think 'horizontal' and 'vertical' refer to the shape or nature of the line itself. In truth, they are BOTH exactly the same type of object: a straight line. Horizontal and vertical merely describe the DIRECTION (orientation) in which the straight line is pointing.

student_says: a slanting line is not a straight line
tilted lines are bent
slanting is a different kind of line
tedhi line straight nahi hoti
if it leans it's not straight
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students confuse 'straight' (meaning no bends or curves) with 'horizontal/vertical' (aligned with the page). A slanting or diagonal line is perfectly straight as long as it doesn't bend. A leaning ladder is still straight.

student_says: vertical line only goes up
you draw vertical from bottom to top
vertical means pointing to the sky
neeche jaane wali line vertical nahi hai
it has to go upwards
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students attach a one-way vector (upwards) to the concept of vertical. A vertical line simply runs up-and-down. It doesn't matter if you draw it top-to-bottom or bottom-to-top; it represents the same vertical orientation.

emotional_triggers: i keep mixing up the names
i forget which is sleeping and standing

entries.subject: maths
entries.title: Introduction to curved lines

classification_patterns.pattern: curved line is just a slanted line
curves must close like a circle
how to draw a curved line
is a rainbow a curved line
gol line ko curve bolte hain kya
yeh curve samajh nahi aa raha
any line not horizontal is curved

student_says: a curved line is any line that is not horizontal
slanting lines are curved
if it leans it is a curve
jo line tedhi hai wo curve hai
diagonal line is a curved line
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students confuse 'not perfectly flat/upright' with 'curved'. A slanting line (like a leaning ruler) is still perfectly straight because it does not bend. A curved line must smoothly bend and change direction as you trace it.

student_says: a zigzag is a curved line
sharp bends are curves
mountain shape is a curve
zigzag line curve hoti hai
if it goes up and down it's curved
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: A zigzag line is actually made of multiple short straight lines connected at sharp corners. A curved line bends SMOOTHLY, without any sharp points or corners (like a rainbow or a smile).

student_says: curves must close like a circle
a curve is a full circle
if it's open it's not a curve
curve gol hona chahiye
only circles and ovals are curves
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students associate 'curve' only with closed shapes like circles. An open bend, like a smile, a rainbow, or a piece of loose string, is also a curved line. It does not need to close back on itself.

emotional_triggers: i can't tell what is curved
mujhe straight aur curve same lag raha hai
why is a slanted line straight

entries.subject: maths
entries.title: Read and write 3 digit numbers up to 999

classification_patterns.pattern: i keep messing up the spelling
how to write two hundred twenty
zero in the middle confuses me

student_says: 045 is a 3 digit number
put zero first to make it 3 digits
099 has three digits
zero se start hone wala 3 digit hai
the hundreds digit can be 0
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students count the physical number of digits written, ignoring place value rules. A three-digit number MUST have a non-zero digit in the hundreds place. If the hundreds digit is 0 (like 045), there are no hundreds, so it is just the two-digit number 45.

student_says: three hundred five is 3005
two hundred twenty is 20020
write 300 then write 5
hundred ke liye do zero lagao
300 and 5 makes 3005
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students write the numbers exactly as they hear them spoken. They hear 'three hundred' and write 300, then hear 'five' and write 5, mashing them together into 3005. They need to understand place value slots (H T O) where digits replace the zeros.

student_says: five hundred twelve is 521
write the 2 then the 1
i get confused between 12 and 21
peeche ke numbers ulte likh diye
teen sau ikkis is 312
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: The 'teen' numbers (11-19) are spoken differently than other numbers (e.g., 'fourteen' sounds like 4 then 10, but is written 14). This causes students to reverse the tens and ones digits when writing 3-digit numbers ending in these values.

emotional_triggers: why does zero mess everything up

entries.subject: maths

entries.title: Observation and identification of unit of repeat in a given pattern

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students pick only a partial piece of the repeating block (like naming only 'star' in a 'star, circle' pattern). The unit of repeat is the SMALLEST COMPLETE BLOCK that, when looped, rebuilds the entire pattern. 'Star' alone would just make 'star, star, star'.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students fail to grasp that mathematical division requires strictly EQUAL sharing or grouping. If 12 sweets are divided among 3 friends, each must get exactly 4. Unequal sharing is not division.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students confuse the roles of dividend (total amount) and divisor (number of groups/size of group), often writing the smaller number first. In division, order matters strictly: Total / Groups = Amount per group.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students think a multiplication fact (like 5 x 4 = 20) only corresponds to a single division fact. In reality, it yields TWO division facts (20 / 5 = 4 AND 20 / 4 = 5) because the divisor and quotient can swap places.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students mistakenly apply the commutative property of multiplication to division. In division, the total (dividend) must always come first. 20 / 5 is not the same as 5 / 20.

entries.subject: maths

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students fail to see the inverse structural relationship, treating them as isolated calculations. Multiplication and division are inverse operations that share the exact same 'fact family' of three numbers.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students confuse the terminology and placement. The product of the multiplication fact (the largest number) must become the DIVIDEND (the starting total) in the division facts, not the divisor.

i always mix up dividend and product

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students believe mental math is about magical guessing or rote memorization without process. Mental computation is actually a chain of small, reasoned steps (like breaking numbers into tens and ones) carried out systematically in the head.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students try to visualize the standard paper algorithm (with carrying/borrowing right-to-left) in their heads, which is very difficult to hold in short-term memory. Mental strategies usually work left-to-right (adding tens first, then ones) because it's easier to track.

entries.subject: maths
entries.title: Mental multiplication of two numbers without use of paper and pencil

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Mental multiplication means no paper at all. Students try to visualize the standard column method in their head, which uses too much working memory and causes calculation errors. The break-apart strategy (split into tens and ones, operate, combine) is designed precisely so that no column working is needed. CISCE examiner reports repeatedly flag candidates who make calculation errors because they rely on visualizing columns instead of using mental-friendly strategies.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students confuse the operation of multiplication with addition when working mentally, often because addition is easier to do in their head. Multiplication is repeated addition, but adding the two numbers just once (6+7=13 instead of 6x7=42) is a fundamental error in operation recognition.

how to add them back in my head

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: When using the break-apart strategy, students successfully split the number and multiply the parts, but their working memory gets overloaded and they forget to add the partial products back together to get the final answer. They need practice in holding one number while processing the other.

this is too hard without paper

entries.subject: maths
entries.title: Estimation of sum, difference and product of two numbers and verification by actually computing them

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: An estimate is meant to be close, not exact. CISCE examiner reports repeatedly note that candidates waste time trying to make rough answers perfectly precise instead of rounding sensibly and moving on. The whole point of estimation is to get a reasonable, near value quickly and then verify later.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students misunderstand the purpose of estimation. They do the hard work of exact calculation first and then round the answer, defeating the purpose of estimation which is to make the calculation easier and faster *before* finding the exact answer.

i can say 100 for 12+13 right
kuch bhi guess kar sakte hain na
estimate means random guess
any number works for estimate
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: While estimation involves guessing, it is an 'educated guess' or a logical approximation based on rounding rules, not a wild random number. 12+13 is about 10+10=20, not 100.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Joining dots with straight segments makes a zig-zag, not a curve. A curved line must flow smoothly and bend gently through the dots, like a rainbow or a slide. CISCE examiners have repeatedly observed that students fail to produce smooth, accurate curves and neat figures in geometry and graph work; they draw choppy straight lines instead.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students think a dot grid is like a 'connect-the-dots' puzzle where every single dot must be used. In reality, the grid is just a background guide. You only pick the dots you need for the corners or the path of your shape. Leaving dots inside or outside the shape is perfectly fine.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: A straight line cannot bend. If a line bends to reach a dot, it is no longer a straight line. Students must use a ruler or visual alignment to ensure the dots they connect form a perfectly straight path without any kinks.

entries.subject: maths

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: The seven pieces can form a square, but they can also be rearranged to form hundreds of other shapes and objects such as houses, animals, and boats. The square is only one of many possible arrangements. CISCE examiners have observed that candidates sometimes fixate on a single expected shape and fail to interpret a diagram flexibly.

pieces ek ke upar ek rakh diye

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: A strict rule of playing with tangrams is that the pieces must lie flat and touch edge-to-edge or corner-to-edge. They cannot overlap or be hidden under one another. Every piece must be fully visible.

do i have to use all 7 pieces
baaki 3 pieces ki zaroorat nahi thi
i left out the square

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: In classic tangram puzzles, you must use ALL seven pieces to form the target shape. If you leave pieces out, the puzzle is not considered solved. All 7 pieces must be incorporated into the final design.

entries.subject: maths
entries.title: Compare two or more shapes to match their properties like sides and corners

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: The number of sides and corners depends on the kind of shape, not its size. A small triangle and a large triangle both have 3 sides and 3 corners. Size changes how long the sides are, but never how many sides or corners there are. The CISCE examiner observations note that candidates often make mistakes linking size to geometric properties.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: In early geometry, a 'side' specifically refers to a straight line segment that forms part of a polygon. A circle has a curved boundary or edge, but it has 0 straight sides and 0 corners.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Rotating a shape does not change its properties or its name. A square turned on its corner is still a square because it still has 4 equal straight sides and 4 square corners (right angles). Orientation does not change the core properties of the shape.

entries.subject: maths
entries.title: Place value and expanded form of number

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: That is the face value, not the place value. The place value depends on the position -- 3 sits in the thousands place, so its place value is 3 x 1000 = 3000. CISCE examiners have repeatedly observed that students confuse the value of a digit with its face value and lose marks; the remedy is to always ask 'which room is the digit sitting in?'.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Writing 3+4+5+6 just adds the face values, which equals 18, not 3456. Expanded form means pulling the number apart into its place values: 3000 + 400 + 50 + 6. You must show the value of the 'room' each digit is in.

student_says: expanded form of 305 is 300 + 50
skip the zero and move the next number up
zero ki koi value nahi toh 5 tens ban jayega

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: When a number has a zero (like 305), the zero holds the tens place. Expanded form is 300 + 0 + 5. If students write 300 + 50, they have incorrectly moved the 5 from the ones place to the tens place. Zero is an important placeholder.

entries.subject: maths

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Only shapes whose sides fit perfectly edge to edge can tile without gaps. Squares, rectangles, and triangles tile a flat region because their straight sides meet neatly. Shapes like circles or random squiggles leave gaps between them no matter how closely they are pushed.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: By definition, a tessellation (or tiling) must cover a surface completely with NO gaps and NO empty spaces showing. If you can see the background between the shapes, it is not a true tessellation.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Tessellation requires shapes to meet exactly at their edges. They cannot overlap or sit on top of each other. Just like real floor tiles, if they overlap, the floor won't be flat!

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: While squares are the most common shape for floor tiles, many other shapes can tile perfectly without gaps! Rectangles, triangles, and even regular hexagons (like a honeycomb) tile beautifully. As long as the straight edges meet and angles add up nicely, other shapes work too.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Triangles absolutely can tile! If you flip every second triangle upside down, they fit perfectly together to make a solid flat surface with zero gaps. Their straight sides match up perfectly.

entries.subject: maths
entries.title: Line-drawings of 3D objects on paper or on flat surface

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: A single rectangle shows only one flat face -- it looks like a 2D shape, not a solid. A line-drawing of a cuboid needs a front rectangle PLUS a few slanting straight lines to suggest the top and side faces, so the eye reads it as a 3D box. CISCE examiner observations note that students struggle to represent depth on flat paper.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: A handspan is a non-standard unit, not a standard unit, because the size of a handspan changes from person to person -- a child's handspan is shorter than an adult's. CISCE examiner reports have repeatedly flagged weak understanding of fundamentals, noting that candidates confuse related ideas like standard vs non-standard.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: The whole point of a 'standard' unit is that it NEVER changes! One centimeter on your scale is exactly the same length as one centimeter on your teacher's scale, or a scale in another country. That is why we use them.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students confuse the names. A centimeter is small (about the width of a fingernail), while a meter is large (about a giant step). It takes 100 small centimeters to make 1 big meter.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Using a meter for small items like a pencil or an eraser is impractical because they are much smaller than 1 meter. You would have to use complicated fractions. Centimeters exist specifically to make measuring small things easy and accurate.

entries.subject: maths
entries.title: Use of measuring tools like scale or measuring tape

The zero mark -- the very first line at the edge of the scale, even before the 1 -- is where measurement must begin.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: A measuring tape is just a long, flexible ruler. While tailors use them for clothes, carpenters and builders use them for tables, rooms, and doors. It is the perfect tool for measuring anything that is too long for a small scale or has a curved surface.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: A scale is designed to measure straight lines. If you try to bend a stiff plastic or wooden scale around a curved object, it will give an inaccurate reading or it might break! For curved objects, you must use a flexible measuring tape or a piece of string.

entries.subject: maths
entries.title: Estimation of the length of various objects and distances in near vicinity and verification by actual measurement

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: A good estimate is a reasonable guess based on what you already know about how long a centimetre or a metre is. If a desk is about 60 cm and a child says '2 cm,' that is not an estimate -- it is a random number. CISCE examiners have repeatedly observed that candidates lose marks when they do not use logical reasoning for estimation.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: An estimate is almost never exactly the same as the actual measurement, and that is perfectly okay! The goal is to be 'close enough'. If you estimate a book is 20 cm and it is actually 22 cm, your estimate was excellent.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: The whole process is 'estimate THEN verify'. If you don't actually measure the object afterwards, you will never learn if your guess was close, and your estimating skills will never improve. Measuring proves how good your estimate was.

entries.subject: maths
entries.title: The relationship between metre and centimetre

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Some children confuse the relationship with the tens pattern they see in counting and assume that since a metre is bigger, it must be 10 times a centimetre. A metre is 100 times a centimetre, not 10 times. Ten strips of 10 cm make 100 cm, which is 1 metre. CISCE examiner observations note this common conversion error.

1cm mein 100m hote hain
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students mix up the direction of the relationship. Centi- means 'one hundredth', so a centimeter is tiny. It takes 100 tiny centimeters to build 1 large meter. Saying 1 cm = 100 m is like saying 1 ant is the size of 100 elephants!

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Meter and centimeter are part of the exact same family (the metric system). They are perfectly related: exactly 100 centimeters fit inside 1 meter every single time. They are just different sized slices of the same ruler.

entries.subject: maths
entries.title: Non-standard units to weigh different objects in the environment

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students judge weight by appearance and size instead of actual measurement. A large object can be filled with air or made of light material (like a sponge or balloon), while a small object can be dense and heavy (like a metal ball). You must use a balance to measure; never guess by looking.

no need to use balance i can tell
looking at it tells me the weight

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students think visual estimation is a substitute for actual measurement. Human eyes cannot measure mass or weight accurately, especially when comparing objects of different materials. A simple balance is required to objectively compare weights by seeing which side goes down.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students fail to realize that for a non-standard unit to be meaningful, it must be uniform. If you weigh an apple using 3 big stones and a mango using 3 small stones, you cannot say they weigh the same. The units being counted must be identical in weight.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students believe counting must always begin at 1 or 0. In math, you can start a counting sequence from any arbitrary number. If asked to count by 10s starting from 43, you just add 10 to 43 (43, 53, 63).

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students misidentify which digit represents the hundreds place, often changing the thousands or tens digit instead. In a 4-digit number like 2350, the 3 is in the hundreds place.

entries.subject: maths
entries.title: Measurement and comparison of the capacity of different containers using non-standard units

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students assume a larger numerical count automatically means a larger capacity, ignoring the size of the non-standard unit used. A bucket might take 80 tiny spoons to fill, but only 10 large mugs. You cannot compare capacities unless the exact same measuring unit is used for both.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students mix different sized units while measuring a single container. To get an accurate measurement in non-standard units (e.g., 'this jug holds 5 cups'), every single 'cup' poured must be exactly the same size. Changing unit size mid-measurement ruins the count.

it is tall so capacity is high
lamba glass hai toh paani zyada aayega
height means capacity

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students confuse height with capacity. A tall, very thin glass might hold much less water than a short, very wide bowl. Capacity depends on the total 3D space inside the container, not just how tall it is.

entries.subject: maths
entries.title: Conservation of volume

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students judge volume purely by the height of the liquid. When poured into a wider container, the water spreads out, making the level lower, but the total amount of water (volume) remains exactly the same. Nothing was added or taken away.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students focus only on one dimension (height) and ignore width. A tall, narrow glass can hold the exact same amount of liquid as a short, wide bowl. Volume is conserved regardless of the container's shape.

entries.subject: maths
entries.title: A calendar to find a particular day and date

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students perform simple subtraction (20 - 5 = 15) without realizing that when a question asks for days 'from [Date A] to [Date B]', both the starting and ending dates are included. You must subtract and then add 1 (20 - 5 + 1 = 16 days).

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students apply 'number line jump' logic (where you start at 0) to calendar days. On a calendar, the starting date itself is Day 1 of your event/vacation. If you are on holiday from the 5th to the 6th, that is 2 days, not 1.

entries.subject: maths
entries.title: Read and write time am/pm and 12 hr and 24 hr clock time

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students leave off the 'am' or 'pm' label, thinking the number alone is sufficient. In a 12-hour clock system, '7:30' is incomplete because it happens twice a day. CISCE examiners deduct marks for missing labels; you must specify morning (am) or evening (pm).

night is pm so midnight is 12 pm
raat ke 12 baje 12 pm hota hai
noon means am
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students associate 'pm' strictly with night and 'am' strictly with day, leading them to call midnight '12 pm'. By convention, 12:00 pm is noon (midday), and 12:00 am is midnight (the start of a new day).

student_says: am is always day and pm is always night
if sun is out it is am
dark means pm
din matlab am raat matlab pm
5 pm is night
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students overly simplify am = light and pm = dark. However, 3:00 pm is bright afternoon, and 4:00 am is pitch dark. AM runs from midnight to noon, and PM runs from noon to midnight, regardless of sunlight.

entries.subject: maths
entries.title: Conversion of 12 hr clock time into 24 hr clock time and vice versa

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students miss the 'pm' label and treat evening times just like morning times. For any pm time (except 12:00 pm noon), you MUST add 12 to the hour to convert to the 24-hour clock. 3:00 pm becomes 15:00.

student_says: add 12 to am times
am time needs +12
subah ke time mein 12 add karte hain
misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students apply the '+12' rule backwards, adding it to morning (am) times instead of evening (pm) times. AM times from 1:00 to 11:59 keep their hour numbers exactly the same in the 24-hour clock (e.g., 8:00 am is 08:00).

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students mechanically add 12 to 12 pm, getting 24. However, 12:00 pm (noon) is just 12:00 in the 24-hour clock. Midnight (12:00 am) is written as 00:00 (or 24:00).

entries.subject: maths
entries.title: Conversion of days to hours and hours to minutes

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students incorrectly apply decimal/base-100 thinking to time. We usually count money and length in tens and hundreds, but time uses a base-60 system. 1 hour is exactly 60 minutes. CISCE examiners flag this as a very common error.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students confuse 'daylight hours' (roughly 12 hours) with a full calendar day. A full mathematical day includes both day and night, totaling 24 hours. To convert days to hours, you must multiply by 24.

However, you need MORE of the smaller units to make up the same amount of time. Big unit to small unit means multiply (2 hours x 60 = 120 minutes).

entries.subject: maths
entries.title: Data collection and its representation in form of pictograph and tables

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students omit the key, assuming one picture always equals one item. CISCE examiners repeatedly deduct marks for this. Every pictograph MUST have a key (e.g., '1 star = 5 students') because the reader cannot guess what the symbol represents or how much it is worth.

if there are 3 apples it means 3 people

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students ignore the key and count the symbols as 1s. In pictographs, a single picture can represent 2, 5, 10, or any number of items. You must multiply the number of pictures by the value given in the key.

har data ke liye alag drawing banani hai

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students try to draw detailed, varying pictures instead of using a single, uniform symbol. A pictograph uses one simple, repeated symbol (like a dot, star, or smiley face) to represent data cleanly. Drawing literal, different pictures makes the graph messy and hard to read.

entries.subject: maths
entries.title: Classification and comparison of data

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students confuse the physical size of the objects with the numerical count of the objects. A group of 10 tiny ants has 'more' items than a group of 2 giant elephants. Comparison of data is about counting how many, not measuring how big.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students fail to sort (classify) items into distinct categories before counting. Classification requires you to put all identical types together (e.g., all red apples here, all green apples there) so you can compare the specific groups against each other.

entries.subject: maths
entries.title: Recording data using tally marks, representing it pictorially and drawing conclusions

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students put the diagonal line too early, crossing on the 4th count instead of the 5th. A proper tally bundle consists of 4 straight lines (||||) and 1 diagonal line crossing them, making a total of 5.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students count the bundles as single units instead of groups of 5. If you see two full bundles and two single strokes, the count is 5 + 5 + 2 = 12, not 1 + 1 + 2 = 4.

entries.subject: maths

entries.subject: maths

entries.subject: maths

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students assume that because a rectangle has 4 sides and 4 right angles like a square, it also has 4 lines of symmetry. However, a rectangle only has 2 lines of symmetry (one vertical, one horizontal). Unlike a square, its adjacent sides are not equal, so folding it diagonally does not produce matching halves.

misconception_signatures.why_wrong: Students think that because a diagonal divides a rectangle into two congruent triangles, it is a line of symmetry. But reflection symmetry requires the two halves to match perfectly when folded. If you fold a rectangle along a diagonal, the longer side overlaps with the shorter side, so they do not align.

While some shapes have the same number for both (like a square), they are fundamentally different transformations. A parallelogram has no lines of reflection symmetry but has rotational symmetry of order 2.
